# To the Honorable, God-
->fearing, Highly Learned, and Most<-
->Prudent,<-
## JAMES COLÉ ORTELIUS,
->*Merchant in London.*<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'E' featuring ornate foliate scrollwork and floral motifs.</image-desc>Honorable, worthy friend, having begun some years ago to draft this accompanying *Treatise*, I have also, on every occasion regarding it, begun to think more and more of Your Honor; as one whom I imagine comes very close in many things to the godly **Apollos** <note>original: "Apollos"; a Jewish Christian mentioned in the New Testament (Acts 18:24) known for his eloquence and deep knowledge of the Scriptures.</note> (who provides the occasion for this entire discourse). For I have good experience of the learned tongue which God the Lord has given Your Honor, to help and advance others in the things of God; as is also evidenced by various edifying little tracts published by Your Honor. However, Your Honor has managed them in such a way that none but your friends have knowledge of them, or know that Your Honor is the author; choosing so skillfully to hide yourself, even as the Lord has given you good gifts to gracefully uncover many spiritual things. In this, Your Honor even surpasses your world-famous uncle, **Abraham Ortelius** <note>Abraham Ortelius (1527–1598) was a renowned Flemish cartographer and geographer, creator of the first modern atlas, the *Theatrum Orbis Terrarum*.</note>; for where he, through his praiseworthy and ingenious labor, uncovers the location and situation <unclear>of</unclear> lands and cities for the service and pleasure of many people who know how to make use of his work—all of which, after all, only serves the convenience of this temporal life—you, by contrast, through your labor, have usefully set before us the nature of our good God along with the bounden duty of men, both in verse,

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedication from Willem Teellinck to James Colé Ortelius. Teellinck, a foundational figure of the Dutch Further Reformation (Nadere Reformatie), is emphasizing that true Christian piety must extend beyond the church walls and into the secular spheres of government, business, and daily domestic life.</meta>

[...practices it,] even at the City Hall, and even during meals—not allowing it to be confined and locked within the doors of the Church, to the unspeakable damage of the soul and the contempt of the Christian life among those who call themselves Christians. For this is certain and sure: that it is the bounden duty of upright Christians, and the earnest aim of all true servants and handmaidens of the Most High <note>original: "alderhoochsten"; a common title for God in 17th-century Reformed literature.</note>. They must seek to present themselves as pleasing to God in all things, and to demonstrate the fear of God that is in their hearts in every trade and every kind of business—whether temporal <note>Refers to worldly or earthly matters, as opposed to eternal or spiritual ones.</note>, spiritual, or in dealings among all people. They must show how high an esteem they hold for the Lord God, so that they seek to reveal themselves as upright zealots for the honor of God and defenders of His laws and ordinances, not only in the Church but everywhere and in all places. 

This is so that, just as they occupy themselves with *all the activities of men, even down to their eating and drinking* (**1 Cor. 10:31** <note>"So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do it all for the glory of God."</note>), these same activities might also be observed and maintained *in all the conduct of men*. In such practice—the right management of ourselves and others—true and upright *devotion* <term>devotie: here meaning a life of active, lived-out piety rather than just religious feeling</term> toward God and Christ remarkably proves and reveals itself. 

As will further appear from the accompanying treatise, if this work might please Your Honor and be of some use and service in further awakening holy and devout reflections toward the Lord Jesus Christ (whom we can never serve enough or to the full) among the children of men, then I shall have all the more reason to rejoice in this labor of mine. Through it, I will have made myself even more useful both to friends and strangers. Firmly trusting in this, I commend Your Honor, along with Your Honor's dear wife, to God and the word of His grace, who is powerful enough to build you both up more and more and, alongside your earthly inheritance, also give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified. Amen; fare well. 

In Middelburg, the first of November, the year 1623.

->*Your Honor’s servant in the Lord*<-

### WILLEM TEELLINCK.

<meta>This page begins the "Preface to the Reader" of Willem Teellinck's work. It follows the dedication to James Colé Ortelius, shifting the focus from a specific patron to the general Christian public. Teellinck introduces his metaphor of the "Key" and explains his editorial method of synthesizing various spiritual writings into a Reformed framework.</meta>

<image-desc>A rectangular decorative woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling foliage and floral patterns centered around a small grotesque mask or face.</image-desc>

## Preface to the Reader.

**I**t has rightfully been observed by all pious Christians how little the multitude of so-called Christians behave in a Christian manner, and how almost all true devotion among the greater part of Christians has completely died out, or is at least confined solely within the doors of the Church. Therefore, the men of God—each according to the gift given to them by God—are accustomed to contribute what they can to improve this; toward this end, we have also designed this present treatise. We call it the **Key of Devotion**: Devotion, just like Religion <note>original: "Devotie ghelijck oock Religie"; Teellinck is explaining the Latin etymology of these terms to his Dutch readers.</note>, is a Latin word and signifies as much as a surrendering of ourselves (namely, to God). This occurs when a person, who previously ran about loose and unrestrained, now places themselves entirely at the service of God and, with a purpose of heart, begins to cleave to the Lord (**Acts 11:23** <note>The original text cites Acts 17:23, likely a printing error for Acts 11:23: "cleave unto the Lord with purpose of heart."</note>) so as to live the time that remains no longer according to human lusts, but according to the *will of God* (**1 Pet. 4:2–3**). Now, toward this we are by nature unwilling, and the things that might move us toward this are hidden and locked away from our eyes. Thus, we have need of them being opened to us; this is done by the Holy Spirit. But He uses the service of men and their labor for this purpose. With such understanding, we then also call this labor of ours the **Key of Devotion**: for in it, we have endeavored—faithfully from the word of the Lord—to open those things which might awaken and strengthen us toward true devotion. Furthermore, it is not required of a key that it be artistically wrought, or made of gold or silver, but merely that it be capable of opening well. Accordingly, we have not exerted ourselves to adorn this treatise with ornate words, but have only endeavored to set it down in all simplicity, just as we thought it might best provide an opening for the student regarding those things that might awaken and promote true devotion within them. 

And because we have also noticed that among so-called Christians, many who still seem to want to behave in a Christian manner are often distracted by the various denominations of Religion (which, alas <note>original: "ochermen"; an archaic Dutch interjection expressing pity or sorrow.</note>, are found among Christians), leading some to adhere to one and some to another, and consequently to read the writings of those authors whom they most favor: so we have taken the trouble to go through all sorts of small books of devotion from all sorts of denominations that we could obtain (even down to the strictest <note>original: "snaarste"; likely meaning the most rigorous or narrow sects.</note> among the so-called Christians). We have gladly gathered all that we found to be sound and from the Holy Scripture—through our own investigation and experience, and from the most excellent authors of the Reformed Church who have written most profitably regarding this—and also from the aforementioned writers, whatever was well said by them and what they had borrowed from the true Religion and sound doctrine. From these we have brought forth material, and that in their own words as nearly as we could; because of this, a change of phrase <note>A change in writing style or terminology.</note> is often found in this book. 

Truly, we have also endeavored to present clearly and edifyingly many obscure things which could easily be misunderstood—and which could not be excused according to the literal word even by their own supporters—and others which were very carefully phrased by the highly-regarded Authors, though with a little alteration. And quite specifically, we have drawn many passages from the book called the *Imitation of Christ* <note>original: "naevolginghe Christi"; the famous devotional work by Thomas à Kempis. Teellinck, though a Protestant, valued this 15th-century text while editing out Catholic elements.</note>, as we have noticed that the same is in the hands of many otherwise well-meaning Christians; yet here and there, certain arguments are found in it which could lead the simple spirit very far astray, away from the right paths of truth. And all this we have arranged with great effort to this end: to give simple, well-meaning Christians an occasion here to...

<meta>catchword: to give</meta>

<summary>Teellinck introduces his "Key of Devotion," explaining that he has synthesized various spiritual writings (including Thomas à Kempis) into a plain-language guide to help Christians live piously outside of church services.</summary>
<keywords>devotion, piety, religious sects, Reformed Church, Imitation of Christ, spiritual growth, biblical living, Christian conduct</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader" from the previous page, where Teellinck began explaining the purpose of his book as a "Key of Devotion." He transitions here from defining devotion to explaining why he has compiled this specific treatise to replace other, more confusing spiritual texts.</meta>

...to give, and no longer to entangle themselves in the investigation of those same writings (which are many, and often very confused, and in many places very obscure, and in even more other places very poorly founded), but rather to hold themselves (if it should so please them) to this present treatise for the revival of devotion. For we can testify with the truth that we believe whatever might be particularly useful for that purpose in the writings of the aforementioned authors—of all sorts of persuasions—has been entirely incorporated by us into this present treatise, and into that which shall yet follow hereafter by God’s grace. 

Thus, this same treatise shall be able to serve (if they wish to view and use it rightly) in place of all other little books of devotion which have been drafted by other authors of all sorts of persuasions. For this also is certain, and stands beyond all dispute for us: That whatever any others may write and publish concerning devotion with great appearance, only the <term>true and right Religion</term><note>original: "vvare ende rechte Religie"; referring specifically to the Reformed faith as opposed to Catholicism or Radicalism.</note> (which we profess by God’s grace) is well-suited to powerfully awaken one to true devotion and to the right practice of a religious life. We also hope that all those who are pleased to investigate this our labor in simplicity of heart shall find this to be true in practice, although we also gladly and without hypocrisy acknowledge that we consider ourselves the least <note>The author uses a humble rhetorical device, "d'oirbaecste keuren" (to choose the most useful/profitable) suggests he is picking the best from others, yet he remains a humble worker.</note> among thousands of our fellow laborers in the **Reformed Church** for this work.

In order to make this our labor all the more useful, we wish to warn the simple reader here of two things.

First, that here and there, some manners of speaking are found from other writers which might be misinterpreted or misused if one did not pay proper attention to the matter itself. To that end, it is necessary that all such manners of speaking—which we bring forward here or there from other writers and which at first sight might seem somewhat strange to the reader—must be taken and understood according to the explanation we have clearly and plainly given regarding those same matters in our other writings, and even in other places in this present treatise. 

So too, to protect the simple reader, we have ensured that they should not in any way excuse the <term>errant ones</term><note>original: "verdwaalden"; Teellinck refers to non-Reformed authors, likely Roman Catholic or Anabaptist mystics, from whom he has borrowed devotional insights while rejecting their theology.</note> (from whose books we have drawn various things in this treatise) in their significant errors, of which they have many. We have uncovered and refuted their specific errors in this same dialogue, and intended to have added it here, but the present treatise became somewhat too large. We shall therefore introduce it, by God’s grace, in the second part (which is already prepared and resting with us). In the meantime, we have nonetheless faithfully revealed and refuted several of their errors and delusions here and there in this present dialogue. 

We have especially endeavored to thoroughly uncover and refute the **delusion of perfection**, in which all the errant ones particularly delight and agree. (This also leads many of them to a perverted view in the matter of **Justification**, which all orthodox Christians brightly profess to place solely in the merits of Christ assigned to us through faith, just as the **Holy Scripture** clearly teaches us everywhere). We have faithfully proven how remarkably they blunder in this delusion, just as we shall also extensively prove in the treatise that is yet to be added here, how lamentably they all likewise blunder in their low estimation of the **Holy Scripture**, while they highly exalt either fabricated tradition or the particular whims of their own spirit.

The second matter about which we deem it necessary to warn the Christian reader here is that he should not let it be imagined as if we were too strict in presenting the necessary **self-denial**, or that we set the path too narrow. For who are we that would wish to do such a thing, since we ourselves—alas!—feel ourselves very weak in every way to properly practice right, moderated self-denial, and daily become sufficiently aware that indeed the **Holy Scripture** requires of the children of men so many, so clear, and also (to the corrupt flesh) so unpleasant and repugnant duties. We consider it sheer madness and rage that the superstitious person, moreover out of their own invention, goes about decorating and designing I know not what strange and new ways, manners, and fashions of life, and even praises them. We hold it for certain and sure that those who do such things, even...

<summary>Teellinck explains that his book synthesizes various devotional writings into a Reformed framework, rendering other "obscure" books unnecessary. He warns readers that he uses language from "errant" authors but refutes their theological errors, specifically the "delusion of perfection" and the neglect of Scripture.</summary>
<keywords>Reformed Church, Justification, Holy Scripture, devotion, self-denial, polemics, perfectionism, religious life</keywords>


--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page concludes the "Preface to the Reader." In the preceding section, Teellinck argued that his book serves as a sufficient replacement for other confusing devotional texts because it is grounded in the "true and right religion." Here, he warns against authors who add their own inventions to God's Word and emphasizes that his instructions are strictly limited to what the Bible requires.</meta>

...by which they can be indisputably recognized as <term>wandering spirits</term><note>original: "dwael-gheesten"; a 17th-century term for heretics or those who strayed from orthodox doctrine.</note>, since they have never possessed even the slightest bit of the true <term>pith</term><note>original: "keest"; refers to the kernel, marrow, or essential core of a matter.</note> and power of Holy Scripture. For had they done so, they would have found so much work everywhere in contemplating that which is clearly and plainly expressed in Holy Scripture, and which is indisputably required of the children of men, that it would never have even entered their hearts to devise anything more, nor to invent something else out of their own minds beyond it, and to impose that upon themselves or others. 

And so that indeed no one should think that we require anything more of the Christian people in this treatise than God does in His Word, the Christian Reader must pay close attention to this: that we truly propose nothing but Scriptural duties, and hold ourselves to them without going any further.

->THE END<- <note>original: "FINIS"</note>

# Key of Devotion. Book I.

<margin><unclear>Principal</unclear> work that man has to do here on earth is that he serves God.</margin>
...and above all to know and understand: why he has been placed here in the world by God, and what work he has to do here.

We are all servants of the Lord, sent by God into the world so that we all, each according to our situation <note>original: "gheleghentheydt," referring to one's station or circumstances in life</note>, should do the work of the Lord our God here, and serve Him with thoughts, words, works, and with all our strength. What is more just <note>original: "billicker"</note> than that we apply and spend the members of our body, the powers of our soul, and all the ability we have in the service of the One from whom we received them? Look at our senses, our understanding, our limbs—it is all God’s, they are all His gifts; He "makes us more learned than the animals of the field," etc. (Job 35:11). If someone plants a vineyard, does he not eat of the grapes? So then, the service of our God is the great work we have to do here on earth: not that God needs our service (Job 35:6–7), but that it is best for us.

Few people pay attention to this now; therefore, many bustle about recklessly <note>original: "onbesuystelyck," meaning without thought or headlong</note> and do almost all

<column-break/>

other things than that for which they were actually placed here in the world. Therefore, consider also what the Lord Christ says to Martha: *Martha, Martha, you are concerned about many things, but one thing is necessary.* (Luke 10:41–42). Pay attention to many people, yet the state of these people is quite pitiful <note>original: "deerlijck"</note>; for it would be much better for us never to have been born, never to have beheld the sun, never to have breathed the air, and never to have trodden the earth, than that we, in the course of our life, should neglect the service of our God—for which we actually received life.

**Appelles.** How could I best take this to heart, for the awakening <note>original: "verwakeringhe," a stirring or revival</note> of the Christian life in me?

**Aquila.** In this way: think often within yourself how you were placed here in the world by God; not to scrape together money or goods; not to chase after worldly honor and high status; not to pursue pleasures and delights; but to serve the Lord your God in everything that you do. Let this then always be before you: that wherever you go or stand, whatever you think, speak, or do...

# Chapter I. 8 Key of Devotion.

be laid down in the Holy Scripture, which we call the **Bible**: in which we receive complete instruction regarding the **will of God**, how He must be served: In such a manner, that even if an **Angel** came from Heaven who wished to teach us something else, we may freely—yea, must—reject him and give no hearing, but hold ourselves to the will of God, revealed to us in the **Holy Scripture**, Galatians 1:8.

Therefore, do nothing in the service of God except that which you have learned from God's word (revealed in the Holy Scripture) that God the Lord requires from your hands. Let yourself be brought under no one’s compulsion further than the Holy Scripture places you under it; and therefore, provide for yourself (if you are not already provided) before all other **household goods**, first and foremost, with a **Bible**. It is the most precious **jewel** that the world possesses; it is the most beautiful ornament that you can have in your house. Also take care that your children learn to read at least enough, and are kept at school long enough, that they can read the Bible. And furthermore, practice yourself therein as well; learn to know each book well,

and the name thereof: So that, when you hear something brought forward from it, you might receive it with all reverence; read it and search it diligently, and accustom yourself to often consider within yourself that the **Holy Scripture** is like a **stately letter** <note>original: "statelijcke brief" - implying a formal, royal dispatch or official decree from a sovereign's court.</note> from the **Heavenly Court**, sent to us by God for this purpose: so that we might learn from it how we must behave and conduct ourselves <note>original: "dragen / en aenstellen" - refers to one's outward comportment and inward disposition before a superior.</note> according to His Holy Will before His high Majesty.

### Key of Devotion. 21 Book 1.

You must not satisfy yourself with the fact that you now have some communion with Him; but you must know that there is yet much more to be found in the Lord Christ, even if you thought you already possessed a very great communion with Him. Yea, even if you had been taken up into the third Heaven (as happened to Paul, 2 Cor. 12), you must still know that there is still more to be found in the Lord Christ than you have already obtained.

And therefore you must always sharpen your heart and urge your soul to seek the Lord Christ more and more. You must forget that which is behind you (just as if you had found nothing at all) and reach forth toward that which is still more to be found in the Lord Christ: in whom all the riches and treasures of God lie hidden.

<column-break/>

unsafe and full of danger.

It happened that he came to me and revealed his intention and necessity, and he wanted advice from me on how he might most securely plan his journey: as he knew that I had made that same trip before, back and forth. I gave him to understand that the way was long and perilous, full of difficulty and toil: That there were many thieves and highwaymen on that road, and also many troublesome, hard, stony, dry, and burning paths: That there were also many misleading spirits there, who, through the bait of present pleasures, great profit, and similar earthly things, seek to delay and entangle the travelers: with many other obstacles and inconveniences besides, so that many were slain on that path, or otherwise died.

He declared to me that he nevertheless had to go there, that his temporal life and well-being depended on it, and that he was also well-encouraged <note>The Dutch "wel getroost" here implies being of good courage or resolute in the face of hardship.</note> to endure all difficulties, however great they might be, if only he might come to Jerusalem with his life preserved.

# Chapter 8. Key of Devotion.

...therefore I would wish, God’s learned Aquila, that you would explain to me somewhat more specifically what I ought to observe, and how I should manage my affairs, so that I might truly—just as I am called a Christian—also conduct myself in a Christian manner at all times.

<margin>Indeed, there are especially four things that greatly advance us in the fellowship of Christ <note>original: "Christi" (Latin genitive).</note>: to conduct ourselves as Christians, namely, 1. the first is that we have good knowledge of the things of Christ, and quite particularly.</margin>
**Aquila.** To that, much could be said; but especially four things are necessary for it, namely: 1. Knowledge of Divine things. 2. Humility. 3. Faith. 4. A holy intention to please God in all things.

**Appelles.** Oh, dear [friend], please explain these things to me more distinctly, and tell me a bit more closely: what things are necessary for me to know and to understand, so that I might conduct myself as a Christian in every way.

**Aquila.** All that God the Lord has revealed in His word is well worthy of our knowing and understanding: for the knowledge of Divine things, revealed to us in the word of the Lord, is like the seed of God, from which godly works must sprout forth, through the grace of God upon us. But there are some things that we especially and above all ought

<column-break/>

to know from God’s word, namely these following:

1. <margin>1. Concerning the nature of our God and Christ <note>original: "Christi" (Latin genitive).</note>.</margin> **The nature of our God.** In that He is one, wise, almighty, infinite God and Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who has created all things, and still maintains and governs them according to His good pleasure, revealing His will for us in our conscience, but especially in His word. Romans 2:15, 16. And even further, that the Son of God became man, and died a cursed death on the cross, to deliver us poor humans from death through His satisfaction <note>original: "ghenoechdoeninge." This is a theological term referring to Christ's payment of the debt for human sin.</note>, and rose from the dead, ascended to heaven, sits at the right hand of God His Father almighty, and prays there for His people, and governs them through His Spirit, and gathers them into a Church, and gives them forgiveness of sins, and eternal life. Hebrews 10.

<meta>This page continues the distinction between types of knowledge started on page 30. While the previous page critiqued "naked" or intellectual knowledge that leads to pride, this page transitions into a description of "spiritual" or "saving" knowledge that transforms the believer's character.</meta>

# Key of Devotion. 31 Book I

Since it is indeed certain that God the Lord reveals His divine things not to play with our intellect regarding them, but so that we might practice them with our lives. Therefore, we must always fervently pray to God the Lord that He would clothe the naked knowledge of His divine things (which we might possess) with heart-felt love for the things we know, and thus warm the cool knowledge with the burning love of the things of God's spirit.

<margin>
Spiritual knowledge, which the Spirit of God casts, is possessed with profound love.
</margin>
The other kind of knowledge may be called **spiritual**: which the Holy Spirit Himself—through a supernatural grace—impresses upon the chosen children of God, namely when we know the divine things, whether many or few, in such a way: that they ignite within us a wonderful love, yearning, pull, and affection of our hearts toward them. So that on one hand, our heart and soul establish themselves upon the known things, wrap themselves around them, remain hanging upon them, and are changed and transformed into the form and likeness of the good, divine things known. But on the other hand, one—

<column-break/>

—has a great horror and aversion toward the wicked and evil things, which are made known to us in the word of the Lord as abominable and rejectable. In such a way that our heart, like a true *Chameleon* <note>The chameleon was a popular 17th-century metaphor for the soul's ability to be "colored" or transformed by what it contemplates.</note>, takes on such a form and movement from the things known, according to what the nature and condition of the known things dictate.

This knowledge ensures that one finds pleasure in nothing more than in the things of God, so that one would always wish to be occupied with them, if such were God's will. Therefore, simple hearts, who first begin to perceive the sweetness of this knowledge, are easily enticed (if they are not warned against it) to neglect the works of their calling <note>original: "beroepinge"; referring to one's daily labor or social duties</note> more than they should.

Now this knowledge alone is a **saving knowledge** <term>salichmakende kennisse: knowledge that is not just theoretical but leads to eternal salvation</term>, and it is such knowledge as someone has of the aforementioned dishes, which he tastes himself and perceives: which are sour, which are sweet, which are **strengthening** <note>original: "confortyf"</note> and **heart-restoring** <note>original: "cordiael"; a medicinal drink believed to stimulate the heart</note>, and which are harmful to health, through his own experience.

->and<-

<summary>The author describes "spiritual knowledge" as a transformative force that changes the soul into the likeness of divine truths, contrasting it with mere intellectual understanding. He warns that the "sweetness" of this experience can sometimes lead beginners to neglect their worldly duties.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the definition of spiritual knowledge as a "lively experience," building on the previous page's distinction between intellectual and heart-felt understanding.</meta>

### Chapter 5. Key of Devotion.

...and a lively experience <term>experientie: a direct, felt knowledge gained through trial or practice rather than just intellectual learning</term>.

For example: When the Christian, perceiving the bitter suffering of Christ, does not only know it as a fact, but knows it in such a way—and sees it in such a way—as if he were actually seeing there his best, dearest, and most beloved friend in the ultimate distress for his sake. Consequently, he is moved toward Christ with holy sorrow (Zechariah 12:10) and with loathing for himself because he has behaved so poorly; yet also with hope, indeed, a trust in grace and forgiveness, because he sees that Christ has paid for everything on his behalf. And all of this is felt deeply. That is a spiritual knowledge. Similarly, when he perceives the wrath of God against the angels, the ancient world, Sodom, and Gomorrah (2 Peter 2:4, Jude 6), he then takes knowledge of it in such a way and observes it so that he is terrified by it until his skin trembles (Psalm 119:120), just like a child who actually sees his father in great wrath and anger. So also, conversely: when he comes to pray, he then knows his God in such a way, in His glory and majesty, that he is touched with

<column-break/>

extraordinary reverence for God’s high majesty, and with exceptional joy and confidence that he may approach Him.

<margin>And often there is a very great feeling and wonderful sweetness in the things of God.</margin>

**Appelles.** I have sometimes felt something of this, and for a time I was so disposed that my heart was so won over to the love of divine things that I found particular delight in them and wanted to be occupied with them always. It reached such a point that my heart, through the overwhelming movement <note>original: "verwarringhe," literally confusion or entanglement, here describing the soul being overcome by intense emotion</note> of love for divine things, distilled many tears from my eyes, having in my heart many holy, burning desires and many quiet, sweet mournings over the things of God. I also became aware that these things cleansed and purified my heart from many impurities and base desires (2 Corinthians 11:7) and caused my heart to melt in wonderfully sweet movements toward Christ. It made my heart pliable, soft <note>original: "dweech," meaning yielding or easily molded like dough</note>, and ready to fulfill God’s will, so that it seemed to me I no longer cared what might become of me, as long as God’s will was done by me and I might please God.

<summary>This page defines spiritual knowledge as a felt, transformative experience where the believer "sees" divine truths as if present, leading to deep emotional responses like holy sorrow or joy. The character Appelles provides a personal testimony of how this divine love purifies the heart and makes it entirely submissive to God's will.</summary>

<keywords>spiritual knowledge, devotion, Appelles, repentance, divine love, fear of God, experience, purification of the heart, submission to God's will</keywords>

# Key of Devotion. Book 1. Page 33.

...but that did not stay with me long / but was very soon forsaken again.

**Aquila.** To be moved in this way / and so touched / by the knowledge of **divine things** / is a proof / that we have more than a natural knowledge of divine things / that indeed the fiery spirit of the Lord / has mixed itself therein / and that there is indeed something supernatural involved / and as for what you say / that you lost that feeling again / the Lord allows this to happen now / and then so that God might teach His children / that they do not have this of themselves / that they are also not masters of it / even when they possess it. For these movements (at their peak) come / and go / according to the will of the Almighty <note>original: "al der hoochsten," the Most High</note>, who awakens them.

<margin>For all of which it is necessary for the Christian to be thankful.</margin>
Therefore it is also necessary for the true Christian / when they feel this same movement in great measure within themselves / to be very thankful to God for it : and also very cautious / to welcome it well / and to cherish <term>coesteren: to nurture or foster with warmth</term> it / and if it then still fades away somewhat / then the Christian person must not

<column-break/>

make too great a fuss <note>original: "misbaer," an outcry or excessive lamentation</note> about it / but he must with patience wait for the Lord / until He shall please to give it again / and come to visit him again / like a friend. And to regain it soon / he must constantly endeavor / to the best of his ability / to always behave in a Christian manner : and in the meantime possess his soul with patience. Do you then also do so / when that sweet feeling of known **divine things** / escapes you / just remain pious / take care / always stand on guard / against the time when the Lord shall please to come again / watch / and pray / have your lamp <note>original: "keerse," candle</note> burning : and it shall go well for you in the end.

**Appelles.** I hope to do so / but tell me yet more specifically / what remains for us to do / and to practice when we powerfully perceive the felt knowledge of **divine things** within us?

<margin>Humble.</margin>
**Aquila.** One must then above all endeavor / to be **humble of heart** : and see to it that one does not exalt oneself because of it / for even the weary **Satan** himself comes at this time / to sniff at our heart / and see if he might find anything...

<margin>Yet / it is found that true spiritual knowledge does not work equally strongly in all true Christians / at all times / whereby it happens :</margin>

### Key of Devotion. Book 1.
<meta>catchword: better</meta>

For no one can live for long in peace and unhindered among men (who mostly strive for high status) unless it be the case that he is content to always be the least and the most despised among the people: in his guild, in the college <note>original: "collegie" — referring to a professional body, council, or social circle</note> where he sits, and with everyone he deals and interacts with.

<margin>Appelles.</margin> But can every person truly judge themselves in this way according to the truth, and deem themselves the greatest sinner, since they cannot all be the greatest sinners?

<margin>Aquila.</margin> In the sense we are speaking of now, that can indeed happen: namely when a person, to whom their own sins are best known, and who rightly through love <note>original: "liefde" — here used in the sense of Christian charity or "caritas," which assumes the best of others</note> must feel the same of others who are also on the path

<column-break/>

to seeking God (for we speak of such people here): that, even if they show some remarkable flaws in themselves, they may nevertheless often have great remorse for those before God, and great struggle, and so forth; and consequently leaves those people to God’s care. Instead, he condemns himself for that which he is certainly conscious of, not daring to condemn others by guesswork <note>original: "gissinghe" — conjecture or estimation</note>.

And here it is worth considering that it is neither bad nor a sin, even if a Christian person (who truly before God—who knows the hearts and minds <note>original: "herten ende nieren" — literally "hearts and kidneys," a biblical idiom (the reins) for one's innermost thoughts and secret emotions</note> and sees and knows all things thoroughly—is better than some others) nevertheless considers himself lesser and more vile than those others. For he must judge not by outward guesswork and suspicion, but by certain knowledge (**John 7:24; Isaiah 11**). Now, he knows himself very well as a poor, vile sinner; another's condition he knows only by guesswork. Therefore, we must still interpret all things for the best according to love; and more fairly consider this: that many, if they had the place <note>original: "plaetse" — referring to one's station in life or spiritual opportunities</note> that we have, would have conducted themselves much

<margin>And to be careful that we do not judge others harshly.</margin>
**Appelles.** I notice then, that you present this as a major point of Holy humility <note>original: "H. ootmoedicheyt"</note>: that one should not be sharp in judging others.

**Aquila.** Yes, indeed; for he who is truly humbled is not accustomed to meddle with judging another man's servant <note>An allusion to **Romans 14:4**: "Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To their own master, servants stand or fall."</note>; but is only busy with judging himself alone, and looking upon himself in this regard as if there were no one else in the world but God and himself.

He also tends to be most humbled and abased over his own sins; and even though he can perhaps see greater sins in others, he nevertheless loathes himself much more for his own sins: and this is quite right, for he knows well that what should grieve and humble him most is that which most hinders him from the fellowship of Christ <note>original: "ghemeynschap Christi"</note> and from his

<column-break/>

salvation <note>original: "salicheyt" — refers to the state of being saved or spiritual well-being</note>: for it is a certainty that the smallest sin we have in ourselves hinders us more in our salvation than the greatest sin of another. And therefore, a truly humble person tends to be more appalled by the smallest sin he commits against his God than by the greatest fault his neighbor <note>original: "even naesten" — literally "equal-neighbor," meaning a fellow human being</note> commits against him. This is a great and very beautiful point of humility when it is well considered. But to grieve most of all over the egregious sins of others, such as those that cause God’s name to be blasphemed—that is called pure <note>i.e., a holy or righteous sorrow for God's honor, rather than a prideful judgment of the person</note>.

<margin>

always view [them] as evil sprouts of his corruption, and vile suggestions of Satan. And following this, a Christian person must also accustom himself to this: that he hopes perfectly upon this revealed grace, **1 Pet. 1:13,** and that he lets himself not be moved from it for any reason—yes, for nothing at all—whatever he might think he hears or sees to the contrary; he must consider it all as merely evil temptations, wicked thoughts, and trials of his faith.

Indeed, even if it happens that to the Christian person, his past

<column-break/>

sins, present failings, and manifold unworthiness come so vividly before his eyes that he must judge himself worthy to sink straightaway alive into hell and be swallowed up by the wrath of God; and even if it be that in this case he is so attacked by Satan that he [Satan] also makes a loud cry in his mind and soul, and stands there constantly and testifies, and says:

> You are mine, you shall before long lie with me in hell, you are already damned by God, I have you already in my power, it will not be long before I come to fetch you:

So still must the Christian person, who now unfeignedly intends to fear and serve his God (for of such a situation we speak here), as much as is in him and as much as is possible: nevertheless hold fast to his blessed hope. He must give more belief to those places of the Holy Scripture which promise all salvation and happiness to those who henceforth wish to serve the Lord, than to a thousand and a thousand such unfounded testimonies of his own mind or of the devil.

# Key of Devotion. Book I.

**Appelles.** I see then, highly learned **Aquila**, that you maintain this: if a person now unfeignedly <note>Sincere or without hypocrisy</note> intends to deny himself and to cling to God the Lord and serve Him as well as he can through **Jesus Christ** our Lord; that he then may—indeed, must—believe that God will be merciful to him for **Christ's** sake, and help him in his good intention, and thus advance him toward salvation.

**Aquila.** Yes, **Appelles**. Yes, I dare to say it, and I know that I speak the truth: If a Christian person is now sincerely resolved

<column-break/>

to cling to the Lord God from now on through **Christ Jesus** our Lord; even if it were so that not only did many troubling thoughts occur to him to weaken this comfort, but that even all the devils of hell appeared to him in visible form—whether sleeping or waking—and all together with one voice testified that he would be damned, and that God would not be merciful to him; even so, the Christian person over all of that must not let his hope fall, nor be weakened in his faith. Thirdly: these people are also found to be very diligent practitioners of the means of godliness; in such a way that, even if they find a wonderful resistance within themselves, they are nonetheless—even against their own will and desire <note>original: "tegen heughe ende meuge," a Dutch idiom meaning with great reluctance or against one's inclination</note>—still spurred on (through an internal, secret power of the Spirit) to devote themselves to it. But now, this much is certain: whatever a person puts great diligence into obtaining, they truly have a great desire for it.

**Appelles.** I understand that now very well, and your reasons flow over my heart like a lovely dew, 

<column-break/>

refreshing me singularly, and assuring me fully that so long as I simply intend, without hypocrisy, to serve my God, and that I do not wish to give in—not at all—to any known sin, I may then firmly assure myself of God’s grace and blessing in Christ my Lord. But tell me now also: what is your feeling regarding those who, giving themselves over to their sins and still living cheerfully therein, nonetheless still firmly assure themselves of God’s favor and grace toward them, and promise themselves eternal salvation through **Christ Jesus** our Lord?

**Aquila.** These same people are quite miserably deceived by the loathsome **Satan**, and are as if captured alive in his snares. *2 Timothy 2:26* <note>The text cites 2:27, but the reference to Satan's snare is found in verse 26.</note> For these believe outside of—yes, against—God’s word, and promise themselves a blessing where God has threatened a curse. For indeed, the Lord witnesses everywhere in His word that He will not excuse those who excuse their sins; that He will be gracious to none of those who are such willful evildoers. *Psalm 59:5* <note>original: "Psal. 59. 6." In many older translations, the verse numbering differs slightly.</note> Now, it is certain 

<margin>
But those who boldly convince themselves that even if they live in sin, God will nonetheless be gracious to them—those have no true faith, but are shamefully deceived by **Satan**.
</margin>

<margin>
4. The last point is that to serve the Lord God uprightly [is to resist] the works of the devil. <note>This marginal note is heavily fragmented in the original.</note>
</margin>

<meta>catchword: certain /</meta>

<summary>Aquila explains that a true desire for God is proven by prioritizing victory over sin over worldly power and by persevering in spiritual disciplines even when it feels difficult. He warns that those who live happily in sin while claiming God's grace are dangerously self-deceived.</summary>

# Key of Devotion. Book 1. 53

Indeed, there are hardly any such willful sinners as those who, assuring themselves of God's grace, become bold because of it and give themselves more easily to sin. These must also believe what specifically concerns them in the Word of God: namely, that they will be rejected by God if they persist in rejecting God’s counsel and do not repent in time. For so says the Lord in **Deuteronomy 29:19, 20, 21**: even if such a person, upon hearing the words of this curse, still blesses himself

<column-break/>

in his heart and says, "It shall go well with me, though I walk according to the dictates of my own heart," thereby adding drunkenness to thirst <note>This biblical idiom refers to adding one sin upon another, or satisfying a sinful craving until it becomes an uncontrollable habit.</note>: the Lord will not be merciful to him, but then His anger and jealousy shall smoke against such a man, and all the curses written in this book shall lie upon him; and the Lord shall blot out his name from under heaven, and shall single him out for misfortune from all the tribes of Israel, according to all the curses of the covenant written in this book of the law.

### Chapter 8. Of the Holy Purpose to serve the Lord God in all things, which is also necessary for us to live a good and Christian life.

---

<margin>
The fourth [point] is that we must have from ourselves [the intent] to live Christianly; that we [act] constantly in all [things].
</margin>
**Appelles.** Tell me now also what the nature is of the **Holy Purpose**, which is also necessary for living a Christian life.

**Aquila.** By that, I mean an unfeigned and sincere desire and resolution to please and satisfy the Lord in all things—great and small, domestic, civil <note>original: "politijcke," referring here to public or social responsibilities</note>, ecclesiastical,

# Key of Devotion. Book 1

...to be done / with a **Holy** / and sincere purpose / of heart to serve the Lord / in all things.

**Appelles.** But is it not / profitable <note>The original Dutch *oorboor* means useful, fitting, or expedient.</note> / that a person / when he has served the Lord for a good while / then also for / a time / serves himself / and the world a bit / so that he / then again with even more / earnestness / and purity / might turn himself to the service of God: / Like someone having somewhat / amused and exerted himself / in that worldly business / in order to thereafter / fall to the **Spiritual work** / of God all the more alertly?

**Aquila.** Not at all. For / the service of the flesh is / not a pleasant / refreshment of the Spirit of / man / toward greater alertness / in the service of God / for the time to come: But / it is a simple suffocation <note>original: *verstickinge*</note> / and corruption of all / the powers of man / in regard to the service of God. **Ephesians 4:22, 23.** so that truly / the more a person serves / the world / and his flesh / the more he becomes / useless in every way / in the service / of God.

**Appelles.** But is it also / possible / that man could always / serve / and please the Lord / his God in everything /

<column-break/>

what he does / and always be able to / serve and please Him?

**Aquila.** We are not speaking now / of what man shall be able / to carry out <note>meaning perfect execution or performance</note>: But what he / ought to purpose / and in that regard it stands written; whether you eat / or drink / or do anything else / do it all to the glory of God, **1 Cor. 10:31.** And **Col. 3:17 & 23.** And whatever you do / in word or in / deed / (do it) all in the name / of the Lord Jesus / giving thanks to / God and the Father through him: / Yes, whatever you do / do it from the heart / as for the Lord / and not for men.

To this it must further / be considered / that the Lord / our God / requires this and that / and all that he requires of us / not because he / has need of our service therein / for he could bring all that to pass / without / us; and if it happens / he does not have / any more because of it / and if it does not happen / he does not have / any less because of it. **Job 34:6, 7.** <note>The text cites Ioh. 34, but the context of God's self-sufficiency refers to Job 34.</note> **Psalm 16:3.** But he requires it / only to test our obedience / when we then / eat / drink / and do all that we / do / that we do it with a respect / for his **high Majesty**, and / at his command / and observing...

<summary>In this dialogue, Aquila explains that serving the world or the flesh never refreshes the soul for God's service but instead suffocates it. He emphasizes that the "Holy Purpose" means intending to please God even in mundane acts like eating and drinking, not because God needs our service, but as a test of our obedience.</summary>

</margin>

</margin>

<column-break/>

every day. Make a good resolution in the morning; and in the evening, examine and reflect upon your life and manners, thinking how you have conducted yourself that day in your thoughts, words, and works, in order to confirm what is good and to improve what is disordered. Act like one to whom the setting of a clock <note>original: "uyrwerck" (hour-work), referring to the mechanical clocks of the period which required daily winding and adjustment.</note> is entrusted, who looks to it daily and winds up the weight every time. In this way, you also take up your Holy intention anew every morning. For just as the weight on a clock, by its own heaviness, pulls downward and descends of itself, so it is with our hearts: being earthly-minded by nature, they always want to sink toward the earth and remain lying still upon the earth, unless we pull them up toward Heaven daily through a renewed intention!

<margin>
4. That we be prudent in the proper arrangement of all our practices.
</margin>

<meta>This page continues the conversation between Aquila and Appelles in the afternoon. Aquila begins to explain the "Key of Devotion" by contrasting the lost "Image of God" with the "Image of the Devil" that humanity now bears due to original sin.</meta>

### Ch. 1. Key of Devotion.

afternoon <note>The text continues from the previous page, where "noon" or "afternoon" was mentioned as the start of the second session.</note> should bring us; that I would show how the God-seeking person might best be advanced to those holy virtues of Knowledge, Humility, Faith, and Holy Purpose, of which we spoke in the morning.

**Appelles.** Yes, that is so, beloved **Aquila**; I would also very much like you to give me some instruction on that, for I find, alas, that I have the greatest need of it.

**Aquila.** I will gladly do that, godly **Appelles**. So you must know that it is necessary, in order to come to the aforementioned virtues, that you especially lay the Knowledge of yourself and of the Lord **Christ** to your heart: and thoroughly ponder and consider how man—who was once created so holy and happy by God, as we touched upon above with a word—is now situated in himself. For many thousands of people please and delight in themselves, and do not even look toward **Christ**, simply because they have never learned to know themselves rightly, nor the Lord **Christ**.

<column-break/>

**Appelles.** Tell me then more specifically, godly-learned **Aquila**, how it stands with man now by nature?

<margin>We are by nature clothed with a completely horrific image, which is further built up by many deadly sins.</margin>
**Aquila.** Man, as he is now situated by nature, has not only lost the Image of God and been stripped and bared of it, but is moreover clothed with the horrific Image of the Devil; which is entirely made and joined together from horrific and damnable sins. In everyone from original sin <note>Theological concept that humanity inherits a fallen nature from Adam.</note>, as soon as man is born; and in those who come to their years of understanding, it is further built up of many deadly sins. This is all the more so because when a person first begins this work <note>referring to the work of self-denial and spiritual turning</note>, they do not yet have any sensible comfort in their Creator, and they must set themselves against the dearest creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" (schepselen) refers to all created things—worldly objects, people, and earthly pleasures—as opposed to the Creator</note> they know.

But as the Christian person now begins to rise against their own corrupted nature, and strives and endeavors to pull their heart more and more away from all worldly things, and to wean themselves from all sinful pleasures and delights which they formerly used to take in created things, the Christian person finds themselves very distressed by it; for they are not well satisfied with themselves,

And where they would gladly take their comfort and joy in Jesus Christ <note>original: "Christo Jesu"</note>, and cling to Him, and rejoice in Him, they nevertheless do not find the power present within them to do so; and that also becomes troublesome to them.

For through the great habit and familiarity they previously had with sin, with the world, and with sinful earthly and fleshly things <note>referring to desires driven by the ego or physical appetites rather than the spirit</note>, these still cling to them so tightly that every time they begin to take courage to go toward the Lord Christ and take hold of Him, these things fall crosswise in between and hinder them greatly, being a major obstacle to them; which then greatly torments and afflicts the God-desiring heart.

**Priscilla.** It is indeed truly so, and the sooner we begin, the better we shall be able to do it. Oh, if only mankind would notice or understand how great a peace and rest they would bring to themselves all their lives long, if they would once thoroughly prepare themselves, in the strength of our Savior Jesus Christ <note>original: "Iesu Christi"</note>, to once and for all thoroughly crucify their flesh with its evil impulses and desires; which now create all the unrest, trouble, and turmoil in human life!

Therefore, those who experience these stirrings powerfully have no need for that time of other physical exercises, such as fasting or other methods usually employed to tame the flesh <margin>1 Corinthians 9:27</margin>. This fire exhausts and subdues the flesh enough of its own accord. 

For this reason, the Lord also tempers these movements and stirrings so that they are not constant over a person; for he would not be able to endure it for long. Instead, He lets them settle over time and become gentler. Because of this, those who have felt this great fire often mourn when it fades, and they "go limping" because of it <note>This is a reference to Jacob wrestling with the angel in Genesis 32:31, where his spiritual encounter left him with a physical limp—a metaphor for the exhausting yet sanctifying nature of intense spiritual experiences</note> like Jacob <margin>Genesis 32:31</margin>.

In any case, this is the truth: when we have these stirrings, if we observe and apply them well, we shall certainly be so advanced by them in the service of the Lord—both in increasing in spiritual gifts and in the breaking down of the **old man**—that by setting ourselves to work in the strength of these stirrings, and betaking ourselves to prayer and other holy exercises and contemplations, we shall accomplish more in a few days...

### Key of Devotion. Book 3.

### 2. Chapter. How we might best awaken the stirrings of the spirit within us, when they delay in coming, by the practice of external good works.

<margin>That we diligently exercise ourselves in all good external works, even when we do not feel inner stirrings of the spirit.</margin>

**Aquila.** If you wish to properly awaken the stirrings of the Holy Spirit and have them enter your heart, you must first and above all encourage yourself <note>original: "vercloecken" — to embolden or rouse oneself to action</note> to this: that you do not neglect the physical and external exercises. For although those are not as profitable as the spiritual ones, nevertheless, when they are practiced with an upright heart, they greatly assist the good stirrings of the spirit. And being easier to carry out than spiritual contemplations (since only a prepared willingness is required to be able to perform them reasonably well), it is very useful and profitable to begin conscientiously with what is easiest. Therefore, always strive and endeavor—even when the spirit does not feel ready in your heart—to do as much good as you possibly can or may, for the

<column-break/>

honor of God, and for the edification and comfort of your neighbor, in your daily calling <term>daily calling: the work or social role God has assigned to a person</term> and in all that you take in hand. And see to it that always, in everything you do—however earthly and physical it might otherwise seem to be—you might through it be further advanced in the power of godliness <term>godliness: (Dutch: Godsalicheydt) a state of living in holy reverence and devotion to God</term> and of the spiritual life. 

With such a heart and purpose, commit yourself also to all external good works <term>external good works: physical acts of service or religious observance, as opposed to purely internal prayer or meditation</term>. If you have the means, give alms; if you have none, give a good example of contentment. Admonish, comfort, and instruct your neighbor; speak for the innocent <note>original: "onnoosele" — can mean the simple, the naive, or the legally innocent</note>; resist the oppressors. Also, be frequent in the external and physical exercises: hearing the Word of God, reading, praying, going to the Lord's Supper, and fasting. Strive to do all these things as much from the heart and in the spirit as you possibly can. And when

<margin>

</margin>
For when we say that each must mostly follow that gift and duty by which he finds himself best [affected]: then that must, according to all divine discretion, be understood with two conditions. First, that the gift and duty are nevertheless given or ordained and instituted by God Himself. Second, that one does not, by following that one thing (by which one thinks one is best affected), stop or suspend any otherwise necessary ordinances and institutions commanded by God. For instance, that one should not let themselves be so taken up with reading God’s word and other good writings that they would therefore neglect the hearing of God’s word <note>This likely refers to attending public sermons or the spoken liturgy</note> or any other institutions of God, all of which we must observe in their proper time. Here applies what the Lord Christ says: *these things you ought to have done, without leaving the others undone* (Matthew 23:23).

### ->Chapter 52. Key of Devotion.<-

...to learn to know the true truth of **God** amidst all those errors.

**Priscilla.** Oh, **Humility**, humility is the key to true knowledge! On the other hand, pride is the mother of all error and delusion. The truth of **God** and humility are like friendly sisters: thus **God's** truth gladly reveals her secrets to humility. Here the proverb also applies: 

<column-break/>

### Chapter V. 152 Key of Devotion.

<columns>

...pledge of His faithfulness to us in His promises, <note>Scripture references: Matthew 28:19 (The Great Commission), Acts 22:16 (Paul’s baptism), Matthew 26:28 (The institution of the Lord's Supper).</note>. 

See, this is presented and confirmed to us in **Holy Baptism** and the **Holy Supper**. From this, it is now easy to deduce that **Holy Baptism** and the **Holy Supper** are a clear and firm testimony to the true Christian that all the promises of the **covenant of grace** <term>covenant of grace: the theological belief that God enters into a relationship with humanity based on His mercy and the merits of Christ, rather than human works</term> truly belong to him, and that he has a part and portion in it. 

So it is that, if any doubt should arise in the heart of the believer concerning these matters, he can quickly be strengthened and find peace by contemplating and reflecting upon his **Christian baptism** and the **Lord’s Supper**. This is because God instituted these to be certain seals of the **covenant of grace**, and allows them to be administered to believers for the strengthening of their faith in the promises of that covenant. 

For when believers see that the Lord God is so earnest in wanting to assure them of His sincere favor toward them—that beyond His word (which stands firm), He has also, in great abundance, instituted **Holy Baptism** and the **Supper**—

<column-break/>

—so that the believer might indeed have strong comfort; it cannot be otherwise than that the Christian, every time he properly reflects on his **Christian baptism** and considers the occasion of the **Holy Supper**, must be further assured of God’s grace and favor toward him. 

It is just like someone who receives not only a bare promise, but also a well-sealed letter <note>The author uses a legal analogy here: while a spoken promise is valuable, a sealed legal document (a "letter") provides much higher certainty in a court of law or business transaction.</note> in which many good things are promised by a faithful and powerful person. Every time he looks at or thinks of that sealed letter, he becomes more and more assured that he has a right to the promised things expressed in the letter, and that they will be granted to him. He knows he will not demand them in vain from the person who promised them, since that individual is both righteous and powerful enough to fulfill the promise. 

And thus we may see how the right use of **Holy Baptism** and the **Supper** serves powerfully to strengthen our faith against all doubts. Therefore, also **Holy Baptism** and the **Supper** [should be approached] with all reverence...

</columns>

**to come worthily to the Table of the Lord.**

Therefore, the Lord does not wish to cast us off immediately, even if we cannot reach the devotion of the aforementioned **Patriarchs** and **Saints**; for the Lord does not look at what we have, but what we would gladly have, and what we embolden ourselves <note>original: <term>vercloecken</term>, meaning to take heart or exert oneself</note> toward, what we seek, and what we contemplate. If you then, still feeling your own unworthiness from observing the high dignity of the **Holy Supper**, exert yourself with the

<column-break/>

most diligent care, in all sincerity of heart, to prepare yourself as well as you can; then you shall be acceptable to the Lord, not according to what you do not have, but according to what you have, and what you would gladly have; for so it stands written: *Blessed are they who hunger and thirst after righteousness, for they shall be filled.* **Matthew 5:6**.

So you must then, in this circumstance, hasten yourself in every way toward the use of the **Holy Supper**. Indeed, you must come to it like a sick person to the **Master Physician** <note>A traditional metaphor for Christ's role in healing the soul through the sacraments.</note>, like a hungry and thirsty person to the living fountain of all righteousness, like a **Poor** man to the **King of Heaven**, to the **Father of lights** from whom all good gifts descend; as one without comfort, to the comfort of all nations. Yea, feeling yourself so very deficient and needy as you are; so must you all the more hasten toward the Lord **Jesus Christ**, from whose *fullness, we can all receive grace for grace*, **John 1:16**; to the restorer of human frailty, and the giver of all inward comfort.

### Ch. V. 182 Key of Devotion.

<margin>And that the Holy Supper is also beneficial for strengthening even the weakest.</margin>
And you must consider this all the more in this way, for experience has taught that the Lord our good God often, at his **Holy Table**, pours out very great comfort and sweetness <note>A common term in 17th-century spirituality referring to a tangible sense of divine favor or emotional peace.</note> into the troubled hearts of his children, against manifold torments and anxieties. Thus the Lord our good God, from the deepest and lowest parts of their own humility and abjection <note>original: <term>verworpentheydt</term>, the state of feeling rejected or worthless before God</note>, lifts them up to the hope of his protection, and delights them from within, and enlightens them with a new grace. So it is that those who, before they came to the table of the Lord, were very anxious, troubled, and sad, without any moving devotion, found themselves afterward—once they had been fed and satisfied <note>original: <term>gheboet</term>, meaning to have a need fulfilled or a hunger stilled</note> with that heavenly food and drink—to be in a better state, greatly transformed and changed.

The Lord also does this so that his children might truly experience and openly acknowledge that they have nothing of themselves; for they find then that, of their own nature, they are cold, hardened, and undevout; but that they are made

<column-break/>

ready, fiery, and devout by God.

Therefore, all devout and God-seeking souls must hasten to the presence of God as much as they can, through all such means as God himself has ordained: assuring themselves that they shall always enjoy some good from it. Who is there that goes humbly to the fountain of sweetness, who does not receive at least a little sweetness from it? Or who is there, standing by a great fire, who does not receive a little warmth from it? Therefore, even if you find yourself in such a state that you cannot scoop with full buckets from the fullness of the fountain and drink until you are satisfied, nevertheless always try to lay your mouth at the source of the **Heavenly Fountain**, so that you might at least receive a tiny drop from it to quench your thirst, so that you do not entirely wither away <note>original: <term>verdoodet</term>, literally "die off," referring here to spiritual dehydration or death</note>. <column-break/>

many other things) very deceitful, **Jeremiah 17:9** <note>original: "Ier. 17. 9." The verse states: "The heart is deceitful above all things."</note>. It often happens that a total child of the world <note>A person focused on worldly pleasures rather than spiritual growth.</note> thinks they have been "very well" at the Lord’s Supper, yet they are simply deceived by the spiritual enemy. This is evident because afterward, in the course of their life, they show no spiritual strength or improvement, despite their delusion that they were "well" at the Supper. 

And so, on the other hand, it also happens that very godly people sometimes think they have been "very poorly" at the Supper, yet one can see that they have indeed been there well; for they are now truly even more humbled, and are lowly and modest in their own eyes than they were before. They are now even more cautious and watchful in conducting themselves well—which are truly very beautiful benefits and fruits of the use of the **Holy Supper**, even if the Lord still withholds the sensible comfort <note>original: <term>gevoelen troost</term>, referring to a tangible, emotional feeling of peace or joy during prayer or sacraments.</note> for which they long so much, and for which they mourn so deeply.

<summary>Appelles admits he avoids Communion because he often feels more "unsettled" after participating. Aquila responds by explaining that spiritual success should be measured by humble conduct and life improvement rather than unreliable emotional "feelings."</summary>

### Chapter V. Key of Devotion.

**Appelles.** So you mean to say, theologian <note>original: "Gods-gheleerde". A respectful title for a scholar of divinity.</note> Aquila, that we should not simply test whether we have been well-prepared at the **Lord’s Supper** <note>original: "Avontmale des Heerē". Referring to Holy Communion.</note> by the comfort we wish to feel, but rather by our reflections and our desires for godliness that we have—or do not have—after we have been to the Lord's Supper.

**Aquila.** Yes, that is what I say, beloved Appelles, and to that you must know—which certainly serves to be well noted—that the Lord God, now and then, gives some of His children certain grace-filled gifts; such as, for example, true faith or closer fellowship with **Christ**, which they nonetheless do not immediately perceive, nor do they even know that they have received them.

**Appelles.** But could that be possible, theologian Aquila?

<margin>
For otherwise the Lord sometimes withholds from His children the feeling of some grace, which He has, however, already given.
</margin>

**Aquila.** Yes, truly, that is certain and sure; just as we know that small children receive life and are born of their mother, and yet they have no personal awareness or discernment of it; and this is not strange if one pays attention to it. For it is an easy thing for God

<column-break/>

the Lord, who knows how to work in us without our doing and without our merits, without having any kind of help from us; also to arrange that same grace-filled work so that we do not notice it, and do not become aware of it. He can indeed keep us unaware of it as long as He wishes, so that we do not feel what He is working or doing in us, until the time that—according to His manifold wisdom—He finds it advisable to reveal it to us for our great comfort.

**Appelles.** Nevertheless, the **Apostle** says: *We have received the spirit which is from God, so that we may know what has been granted to us by God*, **1 Cor. 2:12**.

**Aquila.** That is said of those whom the Lord has pleased to further reveal His works; otherwise, there was a time that even, in a certain sense, the **Apostles** did not know of what spirit they were, **Luke 9:55**. And the Lord does this with some in this way, for He sees and knows that if they immediately found the comfort of the Spirit and the assurance of their salvation in their hearts, they would then become more <note>The catchword "hooger" suggests the next page begins with a warning about becoming "puffed up" or "haughty" with pride.</note>

Therefore, I wish, godly **Aquila**, that you would now also explain to us how we might more and more stir up the fiery movements of God's spirit within us through the proper keeping of the weekly Day of Rest of the Lord.

**Aquila.** To guard that correctly, we must pay close attention to three things: first, what the nature of a religious Day of Rest is; second, for what purpose the Lord instituted the weekly Day of Rest; and third, how we might best reach that purpose of the Lord by keeping the same Day of Rest.

**Apollos.** Oh, please explain these things to us very clearly.

<column-break/>

<margin>
What a religious Day of Rest is.
</margin>

**Aquila.** As for the first: that day which is held as a religious Day of Rest is no longer an ordinary day once it has been set apart as a Day of Rest. Rather, it is in some way distinguished from other days. This distinction does not lie in the day being more holy in itself than other days—for all days are equal <note>A common Reformation-era perspective: time itself is not inherently "holy," but is made holy by its use for God’s service</note>—nor does it lie in us avoiding sin and serving God on that day, for we must avoid sin and serve God all the days of our lives. Nor does it lie in our performing any public worship on that day, for we often do that on many workdays in large cities, which nevertheless are not considered Days of Rest. Instead, the distinction lies in this: that we remember the appointed Day of Rest and therein suspend <note>original: "op-schortten," meaning to hang up or pause</note> our daily work, in order to spend it entirely in religious and Christian ex-

# Chapter V. Key of Devotion.

<margin>
1. The rest that is required of us on the Lord’s day.
</margin>
The holy meditations regarding the required rest consist in this: that we finish all our earthly work during the six working days, so that we might then be free and ready for the work of the Lord on the Day of Rest (Exodus 20:9-10). To accomplish this well, we must especially practice three virtues in the daily labors of our calling <note>Original: 'beroepinge', referring to one's professional or social station in life as a divine appointment.</note>.

**I. Moderation** in our temporal business (Luke 21:34). Namely, that we do not take too much upon our shoulders, nor allow ourselves so much to do that we cannot finish it on the working days; do not let God give way to the world, nor heaven to the earth.

**II. Diligence** in our daily business (Proverbs 10:4). For indeed, the person who goes about lazily or idly on the working days will always find something to do on the Day of Rest. He who wastes his money on trifles and trinkets <note>Original: 'leurderijen ende poppe werck', literally peddler's goods and doll-work, meaning cheap toys or useless vanities.</note> often lacks the same when he needs to buy necessary things; likewise, he who does not redeem <note>Original: 'wtencoopt', a Dutch translation of the biblical phrase 'redeeming the time' from Ephesians 5:16.</note> his precious time from vanities during the week, must necessarily

<column-break/>

find himself short on time on the Lord’s day to properly devote himself to the Lord’s work.

**III. Prudence** in our daily business; namely, that we accustom ourselves to foresee in a timely manner what usually gets in our way on the Lord’s day when it is neglected through carelessness or forgetfulness. This we could otherwise have fended off well enough with a little foresight—as if with a turn of the hand (Ephesians 5:17). Here, surely, a little foresight is worth as much as many great labors.

<margin>
And the exercises that we, while resting on the Lord’s day, must fulfill.
</margin>
The holy meditations that we must take up in order to spend the required rest in holy exercises consist in this: that we consider in a timely way how to keep our heart (which is properly the instrument with which we must do all of God’s works) in good condition for the Lord’s service. Now, the preparation and tuning of the heart to a good tone, as it relates to the observance of the Lord’s day, is especially brought about through these four meditations.

**I.** That we also accustom ourselves to holy exercises during the week...

### Chapter VI. 210 Key of Devotion.

<margin>
1. Earthly and worldly chatter and gossip.
</margin>
...especially should abstain on His Holy Day of Rest <note>Original: 'H. Rustdach', referring to the Sabbath or Lord's Day.</note>, above and beyond our daily work, from these five things.

**I. Earthly, worldly chatter and gossip**, Isaiah 58:13. For the Lord our God is just as much a God of our tongue as He is of our hands; and it is also certain and sure that earthly, worldly conversations <term>propoosten<gloss>subjects of talk or discourses</gloss></term> hinder a person just as much, and even more, in holy and godly meditation than earthly works would. Someone might even more readily perform some worldly work with their hands while maintaining holy contemplations than they could maintain holy meditations while simultaneously carrying on worldly conversations. Therefore, it is truly much to be lamented that it is nevertheless found that there is no day in the week in which more foolish chatter, mockery, backbiting, and idle, useless talk is spoken than on the Lord’s Holy Day of Rest. This must certainly be improved; and to that end, we must avoid the company of idle people. If we are bound by some tie of nature <note>Meaning family relations or close kin.</note> to such people, then we must be intent on turning their

<column-break/>

worldly and earthly conversations toward spiritual and heavenly ones, just as was the practice of our Lord Jesus Christ in John 4 <note>Refers to Jesus turning the conversation with the Samaritan woman from physical water to spiritual "living water."</note>.

<margin>

### Chapter 6. Key of Devotion. 214 ###

[received] from our great God, so it is indeed also quite reasonable that we also apply great diligence to surely keep it as God requires. Now there are primarily four strong occasions and leadings toward the breaking of this commandment, from which we must guard ourselves, namely:

<margin>1. Frivolous company.</margin>

<margin>2. Greed.</margin>
2. Greed, which is the root of all evil. *1 Timothy 6:10*. Consequently, it is the breaking of all the commandments of God; to a greedy person, all the time he spends in the service of God seems like lost time. <margin>3. Splendor and excess in clothing and meals.</margin>
3. Splendor and excess, in clothing and meals. It is true that the Lord's Day of Rest is a glorious and joyful day. *Isaiah 58:13*. Consequently, they are often caused to stay away from Church either in the morning or in the afternoon, or to arrive much too late, to the unspeakable damage of the souls of all people who do so.
