### ->Chapter VI. Key of Devotion.<-

...obey your leaders, Hebrews 13:17 <note>original: "voorgangeren," referring to spiritual leaders or ministers</note>.

See, thus we must discharge our duty everywhere before the Lord in our church-goings; we must indeed remember that the Church where Christians come together is like the Lord's melting-house <note>original: "smelthuys," a foundry or refinery where metals are purified</note>, Jeremiah 6:27, to drive the dross of our sins from us, so that we might all become vessels of honor, 2 Timothy 2:20. Therefore, we must also observe our church-goings to such an end, so that we might be purified there from the dross of our sins; yet we must by no means be like the superstitious who are easily satisfied with the "work performed" <note>original: "gedaene werck," referring to the theological concept of *opus operatum*, the idea that a religious rite is effective regardless of the participant's heart-state</note>, which many named Christians also follow.

For see now for once how it goes there: those same people who just before sat down so modestly and quietly (as it appears) in the house of the Lord before the Lord, Ezekiel 33:31-32, one finds them immediately afterward ranting and raving: shouting and brawling <note>original: "rinckelropen ende rabotten," archaic terms for rowdy and disorderly conduct</note> through the town with a thousand kinds of vanities. The inns, the bowling greens, the archery ranges, the tennis courts, the gambling houses <term>tuysschoolen|establishments specifically for dicing and card games</term>, and the city walls are immediately full and are readily occupied by

<column-break/>

those same people who just before filled the house of the Lord. Do not do likewise! But observe your church-goings as we have just pointed out is proper; and then surely every church-going observed in this way shall do you more good <note>original: "deuchts doen," meaning to benefit or strengthen one's virtue</note> than ten others.

And let this much be said concerning the public and general Holy exercises which we are to observe on the Holy Day of Rest <note>original: "Rustdach," the Sabbath</note> of the Lord.

<margin>The other Holy exercises which are to be observed on the Lord’s day are private or special exercises which one performs at home.</margin>
**Apollos.** Show us then now also which are the private and special exercises that we are to observe on the Lord's day.

**Aquila.** To that end, we must now know in general that all those Holy exercises which we are duty-bound to fulfill on common days—that is, on workdays—ought to be observed by us even more abundantly on the Lord's day. And so it is written in Numbers 28:9-10: On the Sabbath day you shall offer two young lambs...

### Key of Devotion. 237 Book 3. ###

I see also that there is much opposition among the people; therefore I pray you, please point out some means to us by which we might best be strengthened to celebrate and keep the Lord’s Day of Rest gladly as is proper, regardless of what some might say against it.

<margin>Five meditations, or means, to stir ourselves to the proper keeping of the Christian Day of Rest: 1. That we consider that it is God’s will that we keep the Day of Rest.</margin>
**Aquila.** To that end, the following meditations and means are very useful, above the common means of prayer.

First, that we make ourselves understand thoroughly, and urge upon our consciences, that it is indeed God’s will that we should celebrate the ordinary Day of Rest and keep it as a Day of Rest, as was explained above; through this you can be wonderfully helped, if you have but any fear of God in your heart to keep the Lord’s Day of Rest as is proper. This was David’s practice in general against all sin: *Lord (he says) I hide your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you, Psalm 119:11.* Many profane and violate the Lord’s Day of Rest because they forget the commandment

<column-break/>

of the Lord regarding it, or do not urge it upon their own consciences; but instead they look upon the matter only as an indifferent matter <term>middelmatige sake</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, an "indifferent matter" or *adiaphora* refers to actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God, and thus seen by some as optional.</note>, which they may do or leave as it best suits them. See, many are "pregnant" with such a feeling <note>meaning they are filled with or harbor this notion</note>; therefore they treat the keeping of the Lord’s Day of Rest so lightly, and are led away at the slightest occasion from the proper keeping of it. And what wonder is it, when they have no other bond than their own opinion, that they then also profane and desecrate the Lord’s Day of Rest as often as they see fit? They then have no steadfastness, nor any strength in the world to resist when the least battle is brought against them, whenever they allow the necessity of this commandment to be pulled out of their hands. But now the commandment of God imposes a necessity upon us to celebrate and keep the ordinary Day of Rest of the Lord as a Day of Rest. *Exodus 20:8.* This you must then often urge upon your conscience, and make yourself understand well, that it is indeed no indifferent matter...

### Chapter 7. 242 Key of Devotion. ###

...the reason why the Lord God gives us any good, it is nevertheless the means and the way through which the grace, which is freely given, comes into our heart.

**Apollos.** Now I pray you then; show us also how we might best apply this most excellent helpful means.

**Aquila.** For that, you must above all consider what it is to pray, for in this many fail, and therefore also pray poorly.

**Apollos.** Tell us that then, once and for all, properly.

<margin>What prayer is.</margin>
**Aquila.** Prayer is an earnest, ascending desire of the heart toward the Lord God, directed there to obtain from Him what we need, and to thank Him for what we already have: Mark 11 verse 24, Romans 8 verses 26, 27.

Therefore, if a person would pray well, his heart must be made free and loosed from all attachment to and trust in earthly things; and it must lift itself up and ascend to the Lord God Almighty alone. And for this reason, such prayers are also called fiery <note>The original Dutch text breaks the word "vuerighe" across the column: "vye-righe"</note> prayers;

<column-break/>

for just as fire, by its own nature and character, leaves the earth and ascends toward Heaven, so likewise true prayers leave all earthly things and ascend toward God the Lord. And just as we see that in a gun <term>roer: an early type of firearm, such as a musket</term> that is fired, the bullet is driven upward as far as the fire is powerful that ignites the gun; so likewise our prayers go powerfully up to Heaven, in exact proportion to the fire of Holy desire and of the Holy Spirit being powerful within us to drive it forward to the throne of the Most High, from whence it first came: Romans 8 verses 26, 27.

**Priscilla.** That you have also taught me, my Lord; that our prayers are like a smoke-offering, and like the incense of the Sanctuary: Psalm 141:2. But now we know that no incense can climb toward Heaven unless it be thrown into the fire: so then certainly the fire of the spirit and Holy desire is necessary, so that our prayers could ascend from there—

<summary>In this dialogue, Aquila defines prayer as a heartfelt desire that must be "fiery" to ascend to God. He uses the metaphors of rising fire and a fired musket to explain how the Holy Spirit provides the necessary force for prayer to reach the divine throne.</summary>

### Chapter 7. 266 Key of Devotion.

[For thine] is the power and the glory, into eternity. Amen.

All these things are why you have petitioned and prayed to your Heavenly Father in the preceding prayers of the Lord; namely: that the name of the Lord, the Most High God, might be hallowed, His Kingdom advanced, His will done, as well as that His people—and you yourself among them—might be well provided for in all necessity <note>The author uses 'nootduft,' which refers to the essential needs for survival, encompassing both physical bread and spiritual sustenance.</note>, for both soul and body, have the forgiveness of your sins, and be strengthened against the wearying <note>The Dutch 'leydighen' can mean loathsome, wearying, or malicious; it describes the persistent, draining nature of spiritual temptation.</note> Satan, and against all wicked temptations, and thus be delivered from all harmful evil; there are never any things greater than these that can be conceived, nor anything in which God and His people are more concerned or more closely touched. Consider then further what an authority, might, and worthy inclination is necessary in the one whom you worship for these things, and from whom you desire all this, if you were to actually obtain it; and then go further and reflect thoroughly on how, indeed, in God the Lord our Heavenly Father, everything is to be found that is necessary for this; that He is the Authority and has the right to be able to

<column-break/>

grant <term>grant: the original 'ottroperen' is a legal and royal term (related to 'octroi' or charter), suggesting God has the official, sovereign right to bestow favors</term> and allow this, the might and power to be able to give and carry it out, and the favorable inclination to want to give and carry it out. And to assure yourself of this, consider that His is the kingdom, the power, and the glory: that indeed our Heavenly Father, whom we are taught to worship alone, is the rightful King and sovereign Lord of Heaven and earth, with all that is therein: that it is all His (Psalm 50, Haggai 2, Psalm 89) and that He may do with His own what He wills (Matthew 20:15). For His is the kingdom and the dominion over all things, through the right of creation and preservation: and therefore, that He has the authority and the right to grant <note original="ottroeperē">The author continues the metaphor of God as a sovereign who issues official charters or patents of grace.</note> and allow all the previously discussed points of prayer and requests to whomsoever He wills. Consider then further, that just as He has the right to be able to grant such things, He also has the power—having granted and permitted them—to actually carry the same out and put them into effect: for His is the power, yes, to Him alone belongs the power (Psalm 62:12), and there is neither authority nor power anywhere except from Him (Romans 13).

### Ch. VII. Key of Devotion.

<margin>2. Increase of humility.</margin>
2. Increase of humility, or a humble feeling of oneself. Just as when someone compares himself with those who are better than he, he sees his own shortcomings best; so also, when the soul approaches God (who is infinite in all things), then the soul is forced to humble itself to dust and ashes. Then the person sees that there is nothing good in him; all that he has is as nothing <note>original: "niet medaille," literally "not a medal," used here to mean something of no value or not even a small coin</note> compared with that which God has, and that he himself ought to have. humbles the person completely. When a person places himself before God (whatever it might be that he comes to request), he is always immediately aware of what a contemptible thing he himself is, for he sees what a great Majesty God is. And thus, all pride is scrubbed off and driven away through prayer.

**Appelles.** What must I consider before I begin to pray, so that I might pray well?

<margin>1. Before we pray, these considerations are necessary to prepare our hearts well.</margin>
**Aquila.** You must ensure that your heart—which is the tool and, as it were, the musical instrument <note>The comparison of the heart to a musical instrument was a popular 17th-century metaphor; just as a lute must be tuned to play music, the heart must be "tuned" to a state of grace to pray effectively.</note> with which you must acceptably offer your prayers to God—is set in a good tone. To achieve this, beyond sharpening your earnest desire for the thing for which you pray (of which we have spoken extensively above), you must consider these two things.

<margin>1. That we should firmly believe that prayer is the very best means to obtain all desired things.</margin>
First, you must clearly represent to yourself and impress upon your heart that the duty of prayer is a most precious and certain means to obtain and secure a great deal of good from the Lord, the Father of lights <note>A biblical reference to James 1:17, identifying God as the source of all enlightenment and virtue.</note>, from whom all good gifts and perfect presents come forth. You must pay close attention to this and present it to your soul, for there is a very great lack in this regard, even among those called Christians. People find it very difficult to convince themselves and believe, when they are in any significant and felt

<column-break/>

distress <note>original: "gevoelige noot." Therefore, one commonly sees it happen that whenever people see no outward means of help at hand, their hearts fail them entirely, and they lose all courage and hope, just as if there were no God in Heaven who is all-powerful, even without external means, and who said to His people:

> Call upon Me in the day of trouble, and I will deliver you. *Psalm 50:15.*

Just as, on the other hand, it is found that where a person sees abundant means of help at hand, he likewise finds it very difficult to persuade his heart to call upon the Lord his God in good earnest and with all the sharpening of his powers, in all weighty matters, for His help and blessing. Instead, he commonly seeks the help of his God through prayer only weakly, assuming that his cause must now succeed and cannot fail, seeing that he has so many and certain means at hand; no more and no less,

### Chapter VII. Key of Devotion.

For indeed, if we have no permission from God to ask for the things for which we pray, it is then presumption—yes, it is truly great presumption—to desire them; but if we do have permission, it is a great pettiness—considering God’s truthfulness—if we then still harbor doubts as to whether He will grant them to us or not. The question must then be, before we begin to ask: what ground do we have from the word of God to be allowed to ask for such things? If we then find the ground to be good and firm, we must labor to set it beyond all question that we shall be heard. Mark 11:24. <note>Mark 11:24: "Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours."</note>

<margin>
2. When we pray, specifically:
</margin>

**Appelles.** Let me now also hear how I must behave when I am actually engaged in prayer.

<margin>
i. Watch that we do not follow any flying thoughts.
</margin>

**Aquila.** First and above all, you must see to it that you do not follow any flying and wandering thoughts (which might occur to you during prayer) while you are praying. For if you do that, you cannot in any way pray with the heart. Your mouth will speak, and you will not know what you are saying; think then: how would God the Lord wish to

<column-break/>

hear you in your prayers, when you do not even hear yourself because you are led away by vain thoughts?

<margin>
ii. Consider that God the Lord then observes us particularly, and marks how we pray.
</margin>

Secondly, you must then always have this before your eyes: that as soon as you open your mouth and heart to address the Lord your God through prayer, the Lord—the great God of Heaven and of the earth, the King of Kings—also opens His ears and listens to what, how, and with what heart you pray; being ready to answer you according to the condition of your heart. You must thus also in prayer constantly place this great God vividly before your eyes and have your heart fixed upon Him. This must not be neglected; for it is unspeakable what a focus, what a humble reverence, what a holy trust, and what a pure effect the quick observation of the Majesty of our great God is accustomed to awaken in the heart.

<margin>
iii. Strive to be moved each time, according to the nature of the things we bring before God through prayer.
</margin>

Lastly: You must also consequently labor in prayer so that your heart might be moved each time according to the particular occasion and parts of the prayer: specifically, that you [approach] God...

# Key of Devotion. 289 Book. 3.

...that we lift up our hands and eyes toward Heaven, bend our knees, add our audible voice thereto, and withdraw ourselves into a quiet, somewhat dark place, where we find the least distraction through the senses. So it is also useful that, if we find our attention is so short, we also do not make our prayers long. But most helpful for this is the internal preparation of ourselves—namely, that throughout all the time of our lives, we practice setting our hearts more and more loose and free from fleshly desires. For through these (while they are still powerful within us), Satan works the most distraction of the senses. And when we are about to undertake the duty of praying, let us not fall into prayer so <term>abruptly|bottelinge</term> <note>The Dutch word 'bottelinge' suggests a blunt or sudden movement, like rushing into a task without mental preparation.</note>, but beforehand gather our hearts and senses together for a little while, to withdraw them from the world and set them upon our God, before whom we come with our prayer.

### Key of Devotion. 293 Book 3.

...[have offered in prayer] <note>The text continues a sentence from the previous page.</note> various prayers proposed, which are also very useful and profitable for being helped in the practice of praying. And they are thereby prevented from wandering off in prayer into sudden and irrelevant fantasies and requests that are not fitting to be presented before God; into which the weak readily fall who attempt to pray without this help.

And therefore, the simple ones must not think that they are badly off because they are thus bound by such set formulas <note>original: "ghesette formulieren" — pre-written liturgical or devotional prayers.</note> to a certain guidance in prayer; but they should rather think that they are well off, that their weakness is being helped, and that they have a staff by which they might learn to walk. And so this bond leads them to freedom. All the more because they always still

<column-break/>

may—while they use these set prayers—when the Spirit of God becomes ready over them, add more to it and bring in whatever the Spirit of God further brings to their mind.

**Apollos.** So it is your meaning, **Aquila**, that they should strive, through the help of set prayers, to eventually learn to pray by themselves without help?

**Aquila.** Yes, indeed; just as children, who first learned to walk by chairs and benches, becoming stronger, finally walk upright on their own legs without such supports. They take great effort to subdue their corruptions <note>The term "corruption" (Dutch: *verdorventheydt*) refers to the theological concept of human nature being fundamentally flawed or inclined toward sin.</note>, yet they achieve very little.

The confession of a young woman who was very greatly besieged by evil, unchaste desires and lusts: who, on that occasion, withdrew herself for a time from all company, so that for a long time she had not set eyes on any man (as she declared to me); she also withheld from her flesh all pleasant food and drink, fasted often, and always ate but little. And notwithstanding this, she confessed to me that although her body became very weakened by it, the evil desire nevertheless remained very strong and powerful within her, and that the old unchaste thoughts and lusts still constantly presented themselves to her. I asked her whether she had also properly considered her own powerlessness—how little, or rather how nothing at all, she was capable of by herself; and that all the salvation and success of her undertaking had to come from God the Lord, and that God’s blessing was all in all. She admitted to me immediately that she had not paid much attention to that. So I advised her that she should

<column-break/>

pay better heed to that and strive more for the help of God. This she promised me to do, and she came to visit me herself a few days later, testifying to me that after she had begun to take note of her own nothingness and to pay better heed to God’s most necessary help, she had found such a change and strengthening that she had now become almost entirely the master of the evil temptation.

**Aquila.** It is certain that many often put themselves through much effort for a long time, struggling according to the body against their corruption without enjoying much fruit from it; and all that because they neglect to take proper knowledge of their own powerlessness and of God’s sufficiency <note>original: *algenoechsaemheydt*, meaning God's all-sufficient power and grace</note>, and how very much they stand in need of the particular help and grace of God to overcome their corruption. All of whom, if they would take better knowledge of this, and humble themselves thoroughly before God, and confess that they of themselves are capable of nothing at all—

### Ch. IX. 312 Key of Devotion. ###

...from eternity has decided who shall be saved and who shall be lost, and that the precise number of both is already fully known to God; it is therefore altogether in vain to worry about it; for it is already a finished work in God's decree <note>This refers to the doctrine of Predestination, the belief that God has already determined the eternal fate of every soul.</note>. Saying: "if my lot is to be saved, and I am counted among the number of the saved, then I will surely become so, regardless of luck, counsel, or how things go; on the other hand, if I stand among the others, I cannot improve it; God's decree will not be changed for my sake, no matter what I may do."

<margin>
For the Lord God cannot deny His word, wherein He has promised that He will save those who seek their salvation from Him with all their heart.
</margin>

**Aquila.** To this much could be said, but that would lead us too far astray. Briefly, for the satisfaction of the learner, we answer: since it clearly and undeniably appears from the word of the Lord that the Lord God will do good to all those who seek Him (Amos 5:4, 5 <note>Amos 5:4: "For thus says the Lord... Seek Me and live."</note>). Therefore, we must not slacken in our seeking because of the aforementioned claim—even if we hear it said that the Lord God, according to the good pleasure of His will, has made a decree regarding the condition of the children of men;

<column-break/>

nevertheless, we must in no way doubt the goodness of the Lord our God, so clearly revealed to us in His Holy Word; nor should we allow ourselves to think that the Lord God would want to cast out or reject any of those who come to Him from the heart and who endeavor and apply themselves to live and walk according to His revealed will <note>The "revealed will" refers to the commandments and promises written in the Bible, as opposed to God's "hidden will" or secret plans.</note>.

<margin>
And he must also consider that whatever we think of God's decree, there are nevertheless some deep, hidden mysteries within it that we cannot fathom; therefore, we must always direct our efforts toward God's revealed will.
</margin>

Rather, we should hold that God's ways are unsearchable and His thoughts higher than our thoughts (Isaiah 55:8–9); so that certainly, in the nature of God's decree, there are some deep, hidden mysteries that we poor, insignificant humans cannot fathom. Therefore, it is advisable in all things that we should hold (as He Himself advises us in Deuteronomy 29:29 <note>"The secret things belong to the Lord our God, but those things which are revealed belong to us..."</note>) to His revealed will, assuring ourselves that by setting ourselves to work upon the word of the Lord, we shall not labor in vain. For the Lord our God is kind, faithful, and true, who has said: "I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he turn—" <note>This is a reference to Ezekiel 33:11.</note>

Chapter 11. 316 Key of Devotion.

## Chapter 11. How the graceless <note>The Dutch "ghenadeloose" refers to someone who is not currently in a "state of grace" or favor with God, rather than someone who lacks physical elegance.</note> person might be awakened to begin considering God's grace at the first opportunity and with all earnestness.

<margin>
All of which could indeed be improved, if this person only wanted to consider it earnestly.
</margin>

APollos. I do not doubt that you have there opened the true origin of the great negligence which is found in so many concerning the work of their salvation. But now I pray you, tell me also: what counsel would you give, O theologian Aquila, to those who, being entangled in their sins, are still so negligently bound, so that they might take heed of the grace of God which is offered to them from time to time?

<margin>
1. How unseemly it is that the Lord Christ has done so much to re-acquire God’s grace for us, and that we do not care to pursue it.
</margin>

Aquila. To such as still lie so firmly bound and chained in the snares and bonds of their sins, and in the love of the world and the flesh, I am accustomed to advise that they should properly and deeply consider within themselves, on the one hand, how unseemly it is that they should be negligent in so great a salvation; for which the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was content to labor all his life long 

<column-break/>

(Isaiah 53:11) <note>original: "Esa. 53. 11."</note> and to sweat drops of blood falling down to the earth (Luke 22:44) <note>original: "Luc. 22. 44."</note>, yes, to die the bitter and cursed death of the Cross, in order to earn it for us.

<margin>
2. In what a terrifying state all those are who are outside the grace of God.
</margin>

And on the other hand, [consider] in what a terrifying and fearful state all those are who live outside the favor and grace of God; that indeed there is nothing between them and the abyss of hell but only a single thin thread of this temporal life, by which they alone remain hanging and holding fast, so that they do not instantly drop down into the abyss of hell. # Chapter XI. 336 Key of Devotion. #

<margin>1. That the life of grace is the very best and most comforting life.</margin>

**Apollos.** Indeed; whoever would pay even the slightest attention to these things would surely be greatly spurred to break off their sins at the very first opportunity and seek **God’s grace**, so that they might turn back <note>The original Dutch "bekeeren" implies a turning around or conversion of the heart.</note> and escape the coming wrath. Nevertheless, we see that many—who are convinced enough that they cannot last long here—still cannot or will not resolve to seek **God’s grace** from the heart for their conversion. This is because they feel and judge the life of the converted to be a completely difficult and troublesome life, in which there is no joy at all. It is as bitter as death to them to think that they would have to live from now on as they see those people doing who are actually converted to **God**. What advice can you give to ward off this misguided thinking?

**Aquila.** Against this, the person who does not wish to perish through their stubborn and unrepentant heart must surely

<column-break/>

know that although the beginnings of conversion are very difficult and troublesome to the **flesh** <note>In this context, "flesh" (Dutch: "vleessche") refers to human nature's base desires and impulses rather than physical skin.</note>, the life of the converted is not full of trouble and displeasure, as **Satan** the deceiver seeks to convince the unrepentant. Now, the deceit of **Satan** lies in this: he convinces the poor sinful person that—while keeping their old spirit, inclination, and affections—they will nevertheless have to break off, forsake, and let go of their now-beloved whims and follies. This is not the case at all. For that would be not only a completely difficult and tedious task, but also entirely impossible. On the contrary, for the person who sincerely applies themselves to conversion (something I truly wish all people would notice), it stands thus: namely, through **God’s** infinite blessing, they are graced with a **new heart** and a **new spirit**. Indeed, they receive a completely different heart, another spirit: they are clothed with the **spirit of Jesus Christ**, who takes the over- <note>The catchword "d'over-" likely precedes "hand" or "overwinning," suggesting the spirit of Christ gains the "upper hand" or "victory" over the old nature.</note>

<summary>In this dialogue, Apollos asks how to convince people that a life of faith is not a miserable burden. Aquila explains that Satan deceives people into thinking they must change their behavior while keeping their old desires, whereas true conversion provides a "new heart" that makes following God a joy rather than a struggle.</summary>

<keywords>conversion, grace of God, new heart, Satan's deceit, spiritual joy, Apollos, Aquila, repentance, spirit of Jesus Christ</keywords>

### Chapter 11. 344 Key of Devotion. ###

<meta>catchword: HET (THE)</meta>

seeking <note>Continuing from the previous page: "...seeking the grace of God."</note>. That one should do so with proper discretion and moderation. <note>original: "discretie, ende bescheydenheyt." In 17th-century spiritual writing, "discretion" refers to the gift of discernment—knowing how much fasting or prayer one's body and soul can handle without breaking.</note>

**Apollos:** I am of the same mind, divinely-learned **Aquila**; and therefore I now long to understand from you what discretion and moderation must be used therein. I pray you, please explain that to us as well.

**Aquila:** I will gladly do that; but as it is now quite late, and since this matter requires an extensive discourse, it would be expedient that we postpone it until another time.

**Apollos:** It would

<column-break/>

not grieve me, even if your discourse lasted ever so long; nevertheless, I wish that no long delay be taken; might it perhaps happen tomorrow at daybreak?

**Aquila:** Very well, beloved **Apollos**, let it be so; that we might meet one another here again between seven and eight.

**Apollos:** Very well, friendly **Aquila**; we shall not fail to be found here again at the appointed time, by the grace of the Lord, Amen.

# THE
## FOURTH BOOK,

> *In which is treated the Discretion and discernment <note>The Dutch terms "Discretie" and "bescheydentheyt" both refer to the spiritual gift of discernment—the ability to find the "middle way" and avoid religious fanaticism or physical self-destruction through over-zealous fasting or prayer.</note> that one must use in pursuing the grace-filled gifts of God, as well as what comfort and discomfort follows therefrom, according to how it is directed.*

---

->Chapter 1. Introduction to what follows; and what should be noted in general regarding this matter.<-

**Apollos:** Yesterday you promised us, divinely-learned **Aquila**, to explain what moderation one must use in pursuing the grace-filled gifts of God. So now we have come together here again in the fear of God to understand from you what your thoughts are on this.

<margin>In following this, [it is] not our own nature-</margin>
**Aquila:** In general, we must impress this well upon our hearts:

<column-break/>

<margin>-ly impulse, but the precept of God's word.</margin>
that however much we find ourselves driven to seek God's grace, or the increase of it, we nevertheless must not seek it according to our own will, but solely according to the precept <note>original: "voorschrift," meaning a written rule or command.</note> of God's word, without adding to it or taking away from it. For God the Lord knows best how we should exercise ourselves. Many people, not paying attention to this, have invented many harsh ways <note>This likely refers to extreme ascetic practices, like self-flagellation or starvation, which the author views as human inventions rather than divine commands.</note> which God the Lord has not ordained.

Key of Devotion.

**Apollos:** What then is the instruction that we must follow in this, according to God’s word?

**Aquila:** Much could be said on that, and the matter is a heavy and difficult discourse; but to give the best report on it that now comes to mind, it seems to us that these two things (which contain many others within them) must be properly noted:

First, that one learns to properly know the value of the things one has to practice, just as they are considered in themselves: in order to be able to make a true distinction

<column-break/>

between that which is best in itself, and that which is not so excellent; so that we always practice the best first.

Secondly, that one learns to properly know one’s own particular circumstances <note>original: "bysondere ghelegentheyt," referring to an individual's specific life situation, health, and spiritual maturity.</note>, in order to discern clearly from all the good things what is best for us. Since, after all, not all those things that are truly better in their own nature than others are also immediately the very best for this person or that; for the particular circumstances of the person often work something special here.

---

<margin>Learning to know the true value of things.</margin>...to buy gemstones and to trade in them: one must necessarily be able to distinguish which are the best and most precious pearls, and which are not so excellent; if he would trade in them with profit, and set the right value and price on the pearls, in order to subsequently seek and obtain the best pearls most; so likewise, he who wishes to concern himself with the spiritual things of the Kingdom of God, which in the Scripture are compared with precious stones (1 Corinthians 3:12) and pearls (Matthew 13:45); he must likewise exercise his senses <note>Hebrews 5:14: "...those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil."</note> to know which are the most excellent and precious things of the Kingdom of God, and which are not so precious (Hebrews 5:14), so that, knowing the value of these things, he might seek to practice the best with discernment. To this also serves this rule of the Apostle: *Test all things, and hold fast that which is good* (1 Thessalonians 5:21). And for this reason, the Apostle Paul also wishes everywhere so much that all true believers might discern the things that differ, so that

<column-break/>

they might be sincere and without offense until the day of Jesus Christ, being filled with the fruits of righteousness (Philippians 1:10-11).

**Apollos.** I see now also quite well that it is highly necessary, in order to acquit ourselves with discernment in the contemplations of the things of God, and in the fulfillment of religious duties, that one learns to properly know the value of things, in order to seek and practice the best most. But now I pray you; tell us then, by what we shall best be able to measure and learn to know the value of the things of the Kingdom of God.

<margin>Those things are the very best which most partake of the Divine nature, or come closest to God.</margin>**Aquila.** For that, you must know this: that just as God the Lord is the most worthy, so consequently those things are to be valued and esteemed highest which come closest to God, which (if I may speak so) most partake of the divine nature; and this is the best and most certain proof or touchstone <note>original: "toetse," referring to a stone used to test the purity of gold or silver.</note> to properly learn the value of all things, and therefore those things must also be most sought and practiced which come closest to God.

<column-break/>

For truly, what is more reasonable than that God the Lord, who is above all, should also be honored and served above all? And that all things should yield and give place to the things of God to which He presently calls us? And what He now wants done, for His sake, we must then gladly lay out of our hands—all other things, however glorious, holy, and beautiful they might seem to be. For also, if we were still to pursue those things when the Lord calls us elsewhere, then we would not be serving God in those things (even though they are otherwise ordained by God and seem to lead directly to God, such as praying or meditating); rather, we would only be doing our own thing and serving ourselves in them. And following those, one could also expect no kind of blessing from God upon them, nor be able or permitted to draw any kind of comfort from them.

### Chapter 4. Key of Devotion. 354

...to observe. Exodus 18:1, etc. All these duties must then also first be observed and well-fulfilled before one should turn to any particular self-chosen contemplations of devotion.

**Apollos.** But it seems to me, learned theologian <term>theologian: the original Dutch "Godtgeleerde" literally means "God-learned," a respectful title for a scholar of divinity.</term> Aquila, that if one wishes to take the matter this far, then no time at all will remain to be able to start any particular contemplations of devotion for ourselves; for those who have need of support and help—concerning either soul or body—are so many that even if a Christian person had three times more time every day than he has, he would still always fall short in fulfilling that well.

**Aquila.** That is true, God-fearing <note>original: *Godvruchtige*</note> Apollos, if a Christian alone had to care for all the needy—in soul or body—who are in his locality. But now you must know that for this reason there are Ministers, Elders, and Deacons <term>Deacons: Church officers specifically tasked with the care of the poor and the distribution of charity.</term> in the Church of God, whose office is primarily to see to it that people are well-visited in soul and body; but since they are also not capable

<column-break/>

of encompassing everything, all the godly <note>original: *Godt-salighe*; those living a life of active piety.</note> are also obligated to lend a hand; and at least where there is evident need that comes to their knowledge, to run there to help provide for it. **Apollos.** But since it often happens that many are negligent in this, and so the rest must fulfill that, they will nevertheless have no rest day or night.

# Chapter 2. 362 Key of Devotion.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Aquila and Apollos. Aquila is responding to Apollos's suggestion that human effort is useless if salvation depends entirely on God's mercy. Aquila uses the example of a servant's obedience and the fall of Jericho to illustrate that humans must obey God's commands and use the "means of grace" (like prayer and scripture) even if they do not fully understand the divine mechanism behind them.</meta>

### Key of Devotion. 381 Book 4.

...simply because He commands him this or that! Even if it were the case that he could not fathom the reason for the command. What then are we poor humans and **insignificant earthworms**, that we should question our God as to why we must do this or that? Shall we take it upon ourselves to ask Him why we must use these or those means? Must not His command stand above all reason? God says to every person—God commands every mother's child—that they should **diligently pray** to Him for grace; yes, they should earnestly attend to His word for conversion if they wish to be saved. What else remains then, but that we also practice it?

The Lord God wished to deliver the hostile city of **Jericho** into the hands of the children of Israel; yet He commanded them that they should, for that purpose, march around the city several times, blow the rams' horns, and finally also raise a great shout <note>original: "velt geschrey" — a battle cry or public shout</note>, and then the walls would fall down (Joshua 6:4). And what power was there, after all, in these means to throw down the mighty walls of the hostile city? Did it not all depend on the blessing and on the

<column-break/>

secret power of God? Nevertheless, God had commanded it, and the children of Israel had to do it; they did it according to the word of the Lord and thus won the city. Why then should we not also diligently use the **means of rebirth** <note>The "means of grace," such as prayer, reading the Bible, and attending sermons, which were believed to be the tools God uses to convert a person.</note> which the Lord God prescribes for us, even though we know beforehand that the power of conversion is not actually in the means themselves, but in the secret blessing of God?

<margin>Since experience so undeniably teaches that it is not those who despise God's means, but those who practice them, who come to God's salvation.</margin>

And everyone who loves their soul must surely practice God's means all the more to obtain God's salvation; for experience undeniably teaches that although the power of rebirth is in God, nevertheless, children of God are born nowhere else but where these means are practiced. <summary>Aquila argues that humans must use the "means of grace" out of obedience to God's command, comparing the process to the fall of Jericho. ### Chapter VII. Key of Devotion.

If any among us had an arm or a leg that was severely diseased, and for which we ourselves knew no remedy, we would surely be willing to send for the **Surgeon** and permit him to bandage and dress it every morning and every evening, and endure a biting plaster <note>A "biting plaster" was a medical dressing containing caustic or irritating substances intended to draw out "bad humors" or infection.</note> being laid upon it for a time, so that the arm or leg would not have to be cut off, but might be healed and preserved. And we would surely, moreover, pray and sigh to God day and night without ceasing, that He might heal it. Why then should a person—who has an unhealthy soul that could cause him to be eternally cut off from God and cast into eternal perdition—not also permit that biting plaster of sorrow and mourning to be laid upon his unhealthy soul for a time, for its preservation? <column-break/>

livered from eternal perdition, as he is accustomed to undergo trouble, pain, and smarting to have his sore arm or leg healed? How could that ever be justified?

Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep."</note>, stands over it; He is Himself the Master Physician to make it work well for healing for all those who practice it according to His counsel. ### Chapter 7. Key of Devotion.

If any of us had an arm or a leg that was very distressed, and for which we ourselves knew no remedy, we would surely be satisfied to send for the **Surgeon** <note>original: "Chirurgijn"; in the 17th century, this referred to a barber-surgeon who performed external medical procedures</note> and allow him to bind and tend to it every morning and every evening; and we would endure a **biting plaster** <note>original: "bijtterde plaester"; a medicated dressing designed to draw out infection or "humors," which often caused a stinging sensation</note> being applied to it for a short time, so that the arm or the leg would not need to be cut off, but might be healed and preserved. # Chapter VII. Key of Devotion.

## Chapter 8: That the tender and weak children of God <note>A term for new or sensitive converts who lack long-term experience in the faith.</note> must especially take care that they do not easily take offense at the conduct of those who are stronger than they; and that they do not easily accept the evil slanders often attributed to the godly.

**Aquila.** That the tender and the weak must especially seek to exercise this discernment: that they do not easily take offense, nor stumble, at the actions and the conduct of those who are stronger and more gifted than they; and secondly, that they do not easily accept the evil stains and reputations that are often attributed to more robust and better-gifted Christians.

<margin>That they do not easily take offense at the conduct of the strong.</margin>

<column-break/>

appropriate. In doing so, they begin themselves to feel negatively, either toward the truth which the strong profess and uphold, or indeed toward the strong themselves, as if they were profane and godless people. ...which often happens for the sake of such things that truly, in themselves, are not evil, but good, or at least indifferent <term>indifferent: "middelmatighe," referring to *adiaphora*, or practices that are not essential to salvation and thus neither strictly commanded nor forbidden by God</term>. This is truly a great defect; however easily it might happen, and however often it is done, it is a grievous sin. We can gather this from the fact that our dear Paul—who otherwise shows himself to be so tender-hearted toward weak Christians—in this case confronts and punishes them so powerfully and sharply; namely, when they dare to presume to judge and punish others over indifferent matters, speaking to them in Romans 14:3. <note>Romans 14:3 warns those who do not eat certain foods not to judge those who do, for God has accepted them.</note> Just as he speaks in Romans 9:20 to the grumbler against God's eternal election <note>The author compares the sharp tone of the rebuke to Paul's defense of God's sovereignty in Romans 9:20: "But who are you, O man, to talk back to God?"</note>, saying: "Who are you to judge another man’s servant?" <note>original: "wie zijt ghy, die eens anders huysknecht oordeelt?" This specific quote is from Romans 14:4.</note> These words carry and express a great indignation and loathing toward that bold judging that the weak direct against the strong, regarding the use of indifferent things; and quite rightly so. For, whatever one might think of it, it usually arises from great pride and self-conceit.

<column-break/>

Humility shrinks from and fears judging another, and is inclined always to gladly think the best of others; but pride and self-conceit are sharp and bitter in judgment, suspicious of others, and very hasty in rebuking, even that which is well done. But now we know that the Lord Christ teaches us that we must all strive to be humble like little children (Matthew 18:3-4). We must indeed all strive to be clothed with humility (1 Peter 5:5); and this is especially fitting for those who have the fewest gifts upon which they might exalt themselves. Therefore, in every respect, all the weak must take great care that they do not give themselves over to this defect of pride (to which they are otherwise very much inclined).

**Aquila.** And especially they must indeed guard themselves against judging their fellow brother so harshly when they see him doing something they think is forbidden, when otherwise the brother who does so is known to be well-gifted, sensible, and...

3. Regarding the content of the accusation itself.

**Aquila.** Then, thirdly, one must also pay attention to the accusation itself. This is often regarding such things as no human can know, but God alone; as when they persist in crying out against those in whom they see nothing outwardly but godliness and piety, labeling them as feigned actors and hypocrites. This is to judge the heart, which belongs to God alone, *1 Kings 8:39* <note>In this passage, Solomon acknowledges that only God knows the hearts of all human beings.</note>; indeed, it is to judge the heart against all outward signs. This is surely God's work alone: that one should proclaim someone to be a man of an evil heart and a feigned hypocrite, even though one sees nothing in him outwardly but piety and <term>godliness|Dutch: *Godsalicheydt*, a central concept in Dutch Reformed spirituality referring to a life lived in accordance with God's will</term>, simply because he displays that godliness. That is surely altogether unjust; for truly, he who has the inward power of godliness within himself must also display the outward form of it. And he who is virtuous is also perceived outwardly to be virtuous; his own works praise him, whether he wishes it or not, *Matthew 5:*

<column-break/>

16. <note>Matthew 5:16: "In the same way, let your light shine before others, that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven."</note> and therefore, it is a completely unjust dealing that one dares to call those people hypocrites most of all who show themselves most to be very godly people; for it is certain that those who are the most godly, if one pays attention to their ways, must also appear to be the most godly.

Secondly, the accusations that are heaped upon the godly are sometimes so enormous and so extreme that it is easy enough to perceive that they spring from a bitter gall and a gathering of unrighteousness; or they have in themselves so little probability (the Lord God letting them be blinded by their bitter hatred, so that they entangle themselves and are caught in their own words and reasons) that anyone who simply wishes to may see clearly enough that it is merely a fabricated matter, forged solely in a hostile, envious heart that overflows with bitterness. Thus, in order to make the lie better believed, such a heart knows not how to maintain any decent moderation.

**Priscilla.** In that, the bitter Pharisees also overshot themselves against the Lord Jesus, therewith.

# 10. Chapter. That tender and weak Christians, when they properly use the means of growth in spiritual gifts, must then further content themselves in humility with such a measure of gifts as it pleases the Lord God to allot to them.

### Chapter 1. Key of Devotion. 424 ###

it is likewise necessary in the pursuit of spiritual health that one pays close attention to one's circumstances, and the strength of the soul and the mind, and that each must learn to know the measure of his gift, and adjust himself accordingly.

**Aquila.** Yes, that is completely necessary; everyone must learn to know the measure of his gift, and adjust himself accordingly, and put it to work in all sincerity, and then also be content with that: considering that although there is all fullness in Christ Jesus our Lord, nonetheless no one can receive more than the measure of his gift can carry. He who goes to a full and flowing **fountain** <term>fonteyne: used here as a metaphor for the inexhaustible grace of Christ</term> to fetch water can still bring home no more (as everyone knows) than his pitcher or bucket, with which he fetches water, can hold; it is exactly the same with the drawing of spiritual gifts from the rich fountain of salvation of our Lord Christ. <term>Zechariah 13:1; Isaiah 12:3; Jeremiah 2:13</term>

Therefore, here too the tender, yet completely hungry soul—striving for the best gifts and the greatest **godliness** <term>Godtsalicheydt: a life of active piety and devotion</term>—must consider that this is still the greatest and best godliness: that in all parts

<column-break/>

one subjects his will to the will of God, and is content to be whatever God the Lord wants us to be: not only according to the body—sick, healthy, rich, or poor—but also according to the **soul** <term>ziele: the spiritual essence of the person</term>—great or small in spiritual gifts—provided we can find that we have indeed been adopted by God as His children. This we can best perceive by that good **conscience** <term>conscientie: the inner moral sense of right and wrong before God</term>, which makes us practice all the prescribed means of God in sincerity of heart, in order to increase daily in the spiritual life and to arrive at the best gifts. We should then be content that God the Lord extends such a blessing over it as seems good to Him; always confessing ourselves unworthy, even of the smallest of grace-filled gifts.

**Apollos.** So I see then, that everywhere the tender yet hungry Christians, striving after the best gifts, must take note of this: that it is indeed one of the greater gifts of God when one has used the means of God as is proper, and then subsequently remains content with such a measure of blessing as the Lord God is pleased to give to it.

<summary>Aquila explains that spiritual growth requires recognizing the limits of one's own "vessel" or capacity for grace, urging believers to be content with whatever measure of gifts God provides. True godliness is defined as the submission of one's will to God's will, whether in physical health or spiritual stature.</summary>

### Chapter 11. 434 Key of Devotion.

One must certainly pay attention to this; for some infirm <note>original: "crancke," referring to those who are physically weak or have a fragile spiritual constitution.</note> people become faint-hearted when they see that the life of our Lord and the Apostles was very strict and laborious, and when they see some living among them who follow it even better, and find that they themselves are not well able to do so, nor are they inwardly driven to it. Thus they consider themselves far from God, as they do not have a strict life within them. But a person of **good will** shall by no means consider himself far from God because of failings that still exist in him against his will (and against which he struggles daily in all sincerity before God the Lord, who knows the **hearts and kidneys** <note>original: "herten ende nieren," a biblical idiom (see Psalm 7:9) referring to the deepest thoughts, emotions, and secret intentions.</note>), nor because of the infirmity of nature, nor because he cannot practice as much in fasting, in prayer, and in other heavy exercises <note>original: "sware oeffeninghen," referring to rigorous spiritual disciplines like vigils or long fasts.</note>, nor because of any emptiness <note>original: "leedicheydt," implying a lack of spiritual activity or perceived idleness compared to others.</note> he finds in himself compared to others in the service of the Lord or in virtues. In this, the person of **good will** must not be too dismayed, but rather apply himself to this: that he drives out all his failings so far that he, for nothing

<column-break/>

in the world, neither for life nor for death, would want to do anything with a willing heart that is against God's commandment. For as long as he has such a **good will** and sincere intention of the heart before God the Lord, who knows the hearts and kidneys, he has no reason to consider himself far from God; although he cannot do some things well that others do very well. If one only does what one can in sincerity before God, who sees our hearts, then one still proves oneself to be a faithful servant of God.

**Priscilla.** That is indeed true. Thus also our Lord God (which must indeed be properly noted in this) is not accustomed to looking so much at the greatness, righteousness, outward beauty, and excellence of good works, as He looks upon the **ground of the heart** from which those works proceed, and with what intention, faith, and love, and toward what end they are performed. In such a way that some works, which outwardly seem entirely beautiful and excellent, are themselves an **abomination** <note>original: "grouwel."</note> before God, because they do not come from a good ground of the heart. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "good will," emphasizing that the value of an action lies not in its outward scale, but in the internal state of the person and their intention toward God. ### Key of Devotion. Book 4. ###

Wheras other works, which seem entirely simple and modest <note>original: "slecht / ende gheringh," meaning plain and of little worldly account.</note>, such as when a Godly mother cherishes and kisses her little child, are very pleasing and well-acceptable to God, if they occur in faith, with a heart moved toward His high Majesty, and with respect for His commandment and will. Indeed, all works, whether good or evil, derive their particular power and estimation from the foundation, intention, love, and faith from which they inwardly originate and occur; and from the end and purpose toward which they stretch and for which they are done. Therefore, a small work, done from a good foundation of the heart for a good end, is a thousand times more pleasing to God than a great and excellent work originating from a false foundation of the heart and only aimed at self-interest or honor.

<margin>Aquila</margin> Therefore it is also entirely necessary in every respect that the person who wishes to proceed with discernment in the service of the Most High God—who searches the hearts and kidneys <note>original: "herten en niere~," a biblical idiom referring to the deepest thoughts and secret intentions.</note>—should not look so much at what they do, as with what heart and for what end

<column-break/>

they do it; and they should not measure their state so much by what they do, as by what they *are*. For they must first be well-disposed in the heart if their works are to be good. Make the tree good (says the Lord *Christus* <note>original Latin form of Christ.</note>) and its fruit shall be good, *Matthew 12:33.* Many people place their holiness upon a "doing," but that is not the best way. One must place holiness upon a "being"; for however holy our works might be, our works cannot sanctify us. The good fruits that a tree bears do not make the tree good; but the good tree makes the fruits good. So likewise, when we ourselves are holy, then our works are also holy—those which God has commanded us to do—however small and simple they might otherwise be. This includes not only our fasting and our praying, but also our eating, drinking, and sleeping; for as much as they are done out of great faith, to the eternal honor of God, so great they are also. Since indeed everything done for the sake of the great God—even if it were only the giving of a draught <note>original: "toge," a pull or drink.</note> of cold water to a thirsty person—is a great and glorious work.

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the characters Apollos (referred to as Appelles in previous sections) and the theologian Aquila. # Chapter 11. Key of Devotion.

gifted, that they should strive to be clothed with humility, 1 Peter 5:5. Thus giving it to be understood that humility alone—in a person who has already put on Christ through faith (Romans 13:14)—can cover <note>original: "bedencken," here used in the sense of covering or compensating for a deficiency</note> the nakedness of all other gifts that one still lacks.

Therefore, when we lack the strength to practice so abundantly in all kinds of religious contemplations, or if we—having them at hand—cannot perform them as well as others do, let us then humble and lower ourselves over that deficiency; and that shall please the Lord as much as if we had actually followed and carried out those same contemplations.

Indeed, it will please the Lord better that we be humble because we cannot do as much through holy religious exercises as others, than if we did them better than anyone else and were proud and haughty about it. Take from me a common parable.

A Father had two sons, whom he both trained to write well; one was very quick and ready, truly learning well and beginning in a short time to write very well;

<column-break/>

and yet he became so bold and arrogant because of it that he did not feel much gratitude toward his Father for the trouble he had taken with him to teach and train him; the other was very slow and dull to learn, and could not grasp the lesson well; but he was very grieved by this, and often sat and wept because of it under his hat, and went sighing through the house all day because he could not better please his good, loving, and diligent Father in learning the script that was given to him. Which of the two, do you think now, was most pleasing to the Father?

**Apollos.** Undoubtedly, whoever knows what a fatherly heart is knows this also: that the father finds that son most pleasing who mourns and is humbled by his own dullness because he cannot learn his lesson better.

**Aquila.** So also is the Lord our good God inclined toward His children: and therefore, what we lack in those gifts which we would gladly have can be fulfilled through holy humility and

Should he not moderate his pace according to the weakness of the child he has by the hand, or take the child in his arms—Isaiah 40:11 <note>"He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom."</note>—and carry it along the way? What sense would there be in the eye wanting the toe to see as well, or the ear wanting the elbow to hear? Likewise, it is unreasonable that someone, because they have this or that great gift of knowledge, should respect no one except those who also possess it, or (regardless of the weakness of their fellow Christians) always wish to be occupied with high and deep points everywhere, and so confuse them and make them restless. It must not go so in the body of Christ; each has his gifts, and each must [apply] his gift...

### Key of Devotion. Book 4.

...lay them down for the greatest edification; and we must all see to profit from the diversity of the gifts of others, and not use those gifts as an occasion for discord, difference, strife, and disunity; for through these things all good gifts are embittered and made carnal <note>original: *vleeschelijck*, meaning worldly or driven by human nature rather than the Spirit</note>. 1 Cor. 3:6. so that they bring no usefulness to the spiritual life, which we must nonetheless always seek.

**Aquila.** There is indeed much to pray for there, for it has now—alas!—with some almost come to the point where it appears as if the Christian Religion consisted of nothing but disputes and controversies, and that those do the best service to the congregation who are the most fierce <note>original: *alderbloedichst*, literally "most bloody," meaning most vehement or aggressive</note> in disputing, whereas in Truth it is by no means so.

<column-break/>

For as far as the first point is concerned, it is found to be true that there are still many beautiful and lovely things in the Christian Religion to be observed from the Holy Scripture, which must immediately be recognized by all Christians as Divine and edifying, without any disputes; and therefore they can be presented clearly and plainly, without confusion, to the great comfort and edification of the people. These things, however—I know not how it may happen—are noticed, taught, and brought forward by few.

And as for the other point, it is also certain that although it is necessary to refute errors, it is nonetheless found in practice that those who dispute the most do not edify their congregation the best. For it is also certain and sure that the common people do not know well how to grasp where the knot lies <note>the "knot" refers to the core difficulty or the central point of a complex argument</note>; and they often understand very wrongly that which a learned man has driven home with great earnestness.

So it is beyond all doubt that the good congregation can be much better cared for...

->## Key of Devotion. 483 Book 4. ##<-

...distinguishing between good and evil, should now have to push to one side that teaching <note>original: "die reden", here referring to the "logos" or word/doctrine of Christ.</note> which has its beginning in Christ, and all the means through which they came to those well-trained senses; whereas, on the contrary, they must always keep those same things at hand, and use them like a well-ordered wagon to travel further in them and upon them, from virtue to virtue, until they finally might reach the utmost perfection where the prize is set. The translator argues this implies a release of energy or movement rather than abandonment.</note> that which one had held back. It is borrowed from the custom of the Greeks, who placed an overseer over those who ran against each other in the racecourse. This official gave them a signal when they were to begin running, so that they would all set off on the run at the same time, one no earlier than the other, to maintain fairness;

<column-break/>

and he who had that oversight and was appointed to give this signal was called <term>Aphetor</term> <note>From the Greek "aphiēmi", meaning to send forth or release. In the context of ancient races, the *apheter* was the starter at the gate.</note>, which is a word derived from the very same word the Apostle uses here when he says that we must "let go from our hand" the teaching that has its beginning in Christ. By this, he wishes to indicate that we must not throw that teaching out of our hand, but let it loose and set it forward (just as one lets loose the reins <note>original: "de linie", referring to the lines or reins of a horse team.</note> of the horses harnessed to the wagon when one wishes to drive on) in order to travel on toward perfection with their help.

### Chapter XV. 496 Key of Devotion.

In which case the Lord, who is good, graciously accepts the prepared willingness in place of the deed. And this is called the **perfection of parts** <note>A theological concept: like a baby who possesses all the necessary "parts" (limbs/organs) of a human but has not yet reached full "stature" or maturity</note>, just as a child may be called a **perfect human** when it has all its members, even though it is still a very weak and flawed human when it comes to performing the tasks that an adult usually does. Even so, although its strength has not yet fully matured, the child is nonetheless called perfect because it possesses all the parts of a human; and if given time, it shall also grow up into a complete person. 

With this distinction and in this sense, the **Apostle** says to the people of Corinth *that they were not lacking in any spiritual gift* (1 Cor. 1:7). With this distinction and in this sense, the Apostle also speaks of the *perfect spirit, soul, and body* of the Thessalonians (1 Thess. 5:23), even though he indicates clearly enough throughout his letters to those of Corinth and Thessalonica that they were still quite lacking in many ways. They would also reach that state immediately once they had overcome their last enemy, death; for as soon as they have overcome it, they are set free from all the bondage of sin, and are thus taken up to the *spirits of the perfect Saints* (Heb. 12:23).

Thirdly, the **truly reborn** are also called perfect in comparison to others who are either entirely sinful: in this sense, **Noah** was witnessed to be righteous in his time (Gen. 7:1). With this distinction, **Judah** also acknowledged that **Tamar** was more righteous than he himself.

...answers the demand that the Law itself makes for the keeping of God’s commandments.

**Apollos.** Nevertheless, the promises have the commandments of the Law as their subject matter.

**Aquila.** That is true. But the promises themselves, being *Evangelical* <note>Evangelical here refers to the Gospel (from the Greek *euangelion*), meaning they pertain to the news of salvation through grace rather than the strict requirements of the Law.</note>, and founded in *Christ*, neither can nor may be extended any further than what the nature of the *Holy Gospel* brings and works about. In order to understand this well, we must know that two kinds of promises are recognized in *Holy Scripture*: the first, of the Law; the other, of the *Gospel*.

The promise of the Law is simply this: *Do this, and you shall live*, *Romans 10:5*. <note>original: "Doet dit, ſo ſult ghy leven." This is a reference to the legal requirement for life through perfect works.</note> In this way, the Law by no means promises man any kind of strength or help to keep it, but only looks at man as he was perfectly provided for by God in the first Creation, with all the necessary strength to keep the Law. Consequently, the Law only promises life on the condition of such perfect obedience shown to the Law as we have explained above; and no other promise of the Law is known in the

<column-break/>

word of the Lord, nor is any other to be found. And that is the nature of the promise of the Law: to promise no strength for the keeping of the Law, but only to promise life upon the perfect keeping of the Law.

The promises of the *Gospel* are of two kinds: with some, strengthening is promised for the keeping of God’s commandments; with others, eternal life is promised upon that keeping. Both of these promises are *Evangelical*. For as we have just heard, the Law does not promise strength for the keeping of God’s commandments; likewise, it does not promise God’s grace, nor eternal life, upon such a keeping of God’s commandments that is done through a new and supernatural strengthening which one has obtained from God by grace. No; the Law has no knowledge of those things, but pertains only to the keeping of the commandments through the natural powers that were given to man in the first creation. Thus it stands firm that the aforementioned promises are *Evangelical*; so then must also

### Key of Devotion. Book 4.

**Aquila.** That John's reasoning cannot and must not be understood to refer to every kind of sin is irrefutably proven by the fact that the Apostle James <note>original: "Iacobus"</note> explicitly testifies—even of those who are born of God, James 1:18—that they still stumble in many things, James 3:2. And John himself also gives us to understand as much in 1 John 1:9. Therefore, when John says that he who is born of God does not sin, it must be understood in this way: that he does not lead a course of life in sin (just as we recently pointed out that the children of the world are accustomed to doing); that he is, indeed, no "worker of unrighteousness," Matthew 7:21, no "practitioner of sin," Romans 1:30, who are said to "sin" or be "sinners" by way of excellence <note>In this context, "by way of excellence" or "preeminence" means that sin is the defining characteristic of their state or behavior.</note>, John 9:30, Luke 13:2. <column-break/>

—in the preceding verses, 7 and 8: *He who commits sin has neither seen Christ nor known Him; he is of the Devil.* And then he continues with these words: *Whoever is born of God does not sin.* From this it is surely clearly evident that he speaks there of those who lead a course of life in sin; for if one wanted to understand it otherwise, one would have to say that when the Apostle James confessed that he still stumbled in many things, he was then admitting that he had neither seen nor known Christ, and that he was indeed of the devil—which is altogether absurd.

But to understand this even better, we must know that the word **sinning** is used in three ways in the Scripture.

**First:** Simply for the departing from the requirement of God's Law in any work, in thought, word, or deed, even if one only knew of it in the slightest degree. This is called **sinning**, and is a word borrowed from archers, who shoot at a target and miss it; that is then called "sinning," <term>missing the mark</term> <note>The author is referring to the etymology of the biblical words for sin (Hebrew: *chata*; Greek: *hamartia*), which literally mean to miss a target or fall short of a goal.</note> Judges 20:16. Just as if someone shot at a pin and missed...

### Chapter 16. 514. Key of Devotion.

missed by a hair’s breadth, he is said to sin; and it is in this precise sense that the word "sinning" is used by John <note>original: "Ioannes"</note> himself in 1 John 1:4 and by James <note>original: "Iacobum"</note> in James 3:1. It is in this sense that it is testified of all people that there is no one who does not sin, 1 Kings 8:46.

Secondly, it is taken to mean grossly violating the Law of God in one deed or another. Thus David sinned in the matter of Uriah, 2 Samuel 12:9, and the Pharisees sinned against Christ, John 15:22.

Lastly, it is taken to mean making a "course of life" <note>The original Dutch "treyn des lebens" refers to a habitual path or consistent direction of one's conduct.</note> in sin; such that one does not only err slightly or grossly in one act or another, but makes no conscience <note>Meaning they have no internal moral restraint or remorse regarding the act.</note> of sin at all; indeed, one makes a habit of sin and continually occupies, delights, and lives in it. These people are called "sinners" by way of preeminence <note>In this context, "by way of preeminence" means they are the definition of the word; sin is their primary characteristic.</note>. # Key of Devotion. Book 4.

...which the Devil once overcame when it <note>Referring to human nature or the "flesh."</note> stood in perfection; He now knows how to make His children maintain the victory against the Devil in that same flesh, even now that it is so greatly weakened, damaged, and stained with sins.

<margin>Thirdly, so that He might protect them from pride.</margin>
Thirdly, the Lord God also does this so that He might keep us, through that occasion, in true humility and protect us from pride. Behold, the Lord God knows our evil nature <note>original: "quade stoffe," literally "bad material," referring to the fallen state of human nature</note>, and desiring our salvation, He treats us as He sees we must be treated; doing exactly the same with us as we do with a little child when we want to make it love us and cling to us. That is to say: just as we do not immediately give the child everything at once that it would like to have from us, and which we would gladly give it, but we give it some things entirely, and some things in parts, and some other things we only let it see—just as much as we know is enough to instill in the child a will and love for those same things, so that the child loves us, follows us,

<column-break/>

and clings to us. For we well know that if we gave it all at once what we have to give it, it would become proud; it would no longer love us, nor would it cling to us, but it would cling to the things it had received. In the same way, God does not give us everything at once, nor all at one time, what we would like to have from Him, nor even all that He wants to give us. Instead, some things He gives us entirely, some things in part, and some things He only lets us see—and that only as much as may be enough to instill in us the will, the desire, and the love for those same things: so that we run after Him, love Him, and cling to Him. This He does because He knows our nature to be such that if He gave us all at once what He has to give us, we would become proud <note>original: "verhoogveerdighen," to become haughty or arrogant</note>, and thus He would not have from us what He desired, namely: that we should love Him with our whole heart, and that in order to obtain that eternal life, believing firmly, we should [renounce] our own <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword from the previous page was "should," and this page ends by setting up the requirement of self-denial or faith.</note>

<summary>The author explains that God withholds full spiritual perfection from believers to prevent pride and ensure they remain dependent on Him, using the analogy of a parent who gives gifts to a child sparingly to maintain the child's affection and loyalty.</summary>

Might one not say / as I have heard many say / that although the aforementioned duties are all commanded by God / they apply only to the Ministers?

**Aquila.** No / that cannot be claimed with any reason at all. For if the aforementioned duties were commanded by God only to the Ministers / then those would be duties specific to the Ministers / and then the common Christians would not be permitted to fulfill them: just as they may not distribute the Sacraments. <note>In the Reformed tradition, the administration of Sacraments—Baptism and the Lord's Supper—was strictly reserved for ordained clergy, unlike private or group devotions.</note> But now you have yourself sufficiently testified / that you do not doubt / that it is

<column-break/>

free for a common Christian (whenever it pleases him / yet with discretion / as with all other lawful things) to perform the same duties: so they are then not commanded to the Ministers alone / but also to all Christians.

**Apollos.** I can say nothing at all against this: But even so, you must surely admit this to me; that the aforementioned duties / although they concern all Christians / primarily apply to the Ministers.

**Aquila.** I cannot do that without distinction / but I will tell you how it is: A certain distinction must be made between the aforementioned duties; for some of them / do seem to concern the Ministers somewhat more specifically / but the rest certainly apply just as much to common Christians / if not more / than to the Ministers.

**Apollos.** Give me some further instruction on that.

**Aquila.** The general rule is / those duties which concern our own person / apply to us just as much / as to the Ministers. Duties which we owe to our fellow neighbors / seem to concern the Ministers somewhat more.

**Apollos.** Yes, I see that now to some extent; but you must certainly also admit this: that the Ministers, notwithstanding that, have a certain advantage here. ## Chapter XVIII.

->Of whatever state or calling we may be, we must<-
->always consider the Spiritual more than the<-
