<margin>Yet all Christians are always obliged to seek spiritual and Heavenly things above all.</margin>
**Aquila.** That is true, godly Apollos; nevertheless, they are all obliged to seek the Kingdom of God first and foremost (Matthew 6:33 <note>The original text cites Matthew 6:23, though the context of "seeking first the Kingdom" refers to verse 33.</note>), and not to labor so much for the food that perishes, as for the food that remains unto eternal life (John 6:27). For so the Lord teaches us, who has command over us all; the matter itself also demonstrates this everywhere. We must all certainly acknowledge that spiritual things are by far the best: and we have proven above that the best things must be sought most. Thus we must surely and rightly practice how we might more and more detach ourselves from earthly business, in order to contemplate Heavenly goods, which are that better and lasting wealth (Hebrews 10:34), and we must all alike, of whatever calling or state we may be, diligently examine and learn how little

<column-break/>

we need to <term>clutter</term> <note>original: "beslobberen" — to soil or entangle oneself with messy or mundane tasks.</note> ourselves with earthly things, so as to devote ourselves to seeking heavenly goods through the practice of all kinds of holy exercises of <term>devotion</term> <note>original: "devotie" — here meaning a lifestyle of dedicated religious practice and prayer.</note>. We spoke before of some who go so far in this that they <term>abandon everything entirely</term> <note>original: "upt een ende upt al schepden"</note> and stick their heads in a <term>cloister</term> <note>original: "Clooster" — a monastery or convent.</note>, and withdraw themselves so completely from all temporal business. These (as we heard) go beyond the proper measure; for in doing so, they withdraw their service from the <term>common good</term> <note>original: "ghemepne saecke"</note> and the church, which they are duty-bound to serve: not only through persistence in prayer, but also through other considerations, as all upright, God-zealous people have done. Nevertheless, avoiding their mistake, we ought to holily consider how little we need to involve ourselves in the world.

Chapter XXIII. Key of Devotion.

<margin>And they are obliged to study this: how much they might involve themselves in earthly things and how little in the spiritual; but rather, how much they ought to involve themselves in spiritual things, and how little in the earthly.</margin>

### Key of Devotion.

**Apollos.** I cannot well restrain myself when I see these things taking place among those called Christians; I often think then, where are our senses, and what comes over us, that we do not listen better to what the Lord Christ stands and cries out: **Seek first the Kingdom of God, and his righteousness, and all other things shall be added unto you**, Matthew 6:33. Often I also think to myself: what will Christians do for the Lord Christ (whom they call their Dear Lord) if they will not do this? If they will not do so much as to pull their hands away from their work when he stands by them and calls out: **Work not for the food that perishes, but for that food which remains unto eternal life** <note>original: "Werckt niet om de spijse die vergaet, maer om die spijse die blijft tot in het eewighe leven" — a reference to John 6:27.</note>. Is working then such a pleasant thing? Is slaving and laboring such a lovely matter that we refuse to leave it be, even though the Savior of our souls calls us away from the work? Had he burdened us with something heavy, we still ought to do what he asked; but now, when he merely bids us not to work—that is, not to work too much for that food which perishes—how could

<column-break/>

we wish for anything more beautiful? It was laid as a curse upon our first Ancestors, after they had sinned, that they must labor hard for their **daily bread** <note>original: "Broodt cost" — literally "bread-cost," meaning the basic necessities required to sustain life.</note>, Genesis 3:19. The Lord Christ comes with his **gentle yoke** <note>A reference to Matthew 11:30: "For my yoke is easy and my burden is light."</note> and wishes to relieve us somewhat even of this: and shall we be so senseless that we would nonetheless want to keep that hard yoke upon our necks? Is it not unnatural? Who ever saw an Ox or a Horse that was not glad to be unhitched from the plow? What a new kind of **obstinacy** <note>original: "block" — literally a block of wood or a clog; used here to describe a heavy, self-imposed burden or a stubborn mental block.</note> is this then, that one continues slaving when one may rest? That one still wants to keep working, when we may be excused from the hard labor?

**Priscilla.** Truly, it must make a person stand amazed who pays proper attention to this; and all the more so when one observes for the sake of what things the foolish multitude slave and overwork themselves so much. The majority do not bustle so busily for their daily bread simply to sustain their lives—which might seem to be somewhat excusable, for **skin for skin, a man will give all that he has for** <note>A reference to Job 2:4, implying people will do anything to save their lives.</note>

**Aquila.** The Lord Christ speaks so decisively in opposition to the excessively great and violent bustle of men in searching for the food that perishes. Just as when we see someone doing something too hastily—which must indeed be done, but not with such intensity—we cry out, "do not do that!" So it is also common in Holy Scripture to say a thing absolutely, which is nonetheless disapproved of more in a comparative sense, such as in **1 Corinthians 1:17** <note>original reference to Paul saying Christ sent him not to baptize, but to preach—a comparative emphasis rather than a literal prohibition</note> and **Genesis 32:28**. When the Lord Christ then says, *do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that remains until eternal life*, He gives it to be understood that we must labor so very diligently and earnestly for the food that remains, that in comparison to it, our labor and work for the food that perishes might appear as if it were considered no work at all.

Each day and night have only twenty-four hours together, and each person has only six days in the week to labor, and within that time people must—according to God's command—see that they provide themselves with all the temporal things that they have need of, and each must contribute his part: for thus it stands written, *that if any would not work, neither should he eat,* **2 Thessalonians 3:10**. If now many people are occupied during the six days of the week with excesses and superfluities <note>original: "superfluïtepten"; luxury goods or unnecessary items.</note>, which only serve to provide for the flesh according to its lusts; then necessarily the rest of the people, who remain to provide for necessary things, must have their work much harder before they can finish it: for as our proverb says, *many hands make light work.* If one then draws many hands away from necessary works toward superfluities, then those remaining to work on necessary things will necessarily have to spend much more time to provide them. <column-break/>

Now that burdens the work and robs the spiritual; for it causes people to necessarily spend much more time on the temporal. ### Key of Devotion. 357. Book 4.

<margin>
And however much we might have to do with constant busywork in our idle affairs, we must nevertheless not neglect to set ourselves apart at least once a day to give ourselves entirely to God.

**Secondly**, this must always remain a firm rule: that no matter how much or how little we have to do, we must always turn ourselves away from all worldly business at least once a day. We should make ourselves as completely free and liberated from all earthly and temporal concerns as we possibly can, in order to give ourselves entirely and exclusively, with both understanding and affection, to the Lord our God alone (1 Chronicles 22:19). <note>The original citation says 2 Chronicles, but the context of seeking God with the heart matches 1 Chronicles 22:19.</note> Following this, we must also place ourselves at least once a day in the majestic presence of God and then give ourselves over to Him completely—without any hesitation, worldly regard, or reservation—so that from now on we may live uprightly (as we are indeed bound to do) and solely according to God's will. We should conduct all our affairs by subjecting, surrendering, and laying ourselves down as a sacrificial offering <note>original: "gheslacht offerhande" - literally a slaughtered sacrifice, emphasizing total surrender</note> (Romans 12:1) into the hand and the good will of our good God. We must be whatever He wants us to be: in prosperity and adversity, in honor or contempt, in loss, in gain, and in all things. And to better win over our hearts to this end,

<column-break/>

<margin>
And to always be diligent in this arrangement, we [must consider] the allocation of time for spiritual things.
</margin>

we must also strive to bring together and make a gathering of all God's benefits shown to us: in Creation, in His general sustenance, in general redemption, and in the daily care shown to our souls and bodies. We should reflect on the thousands upon thousands of good things that the Lord still allows us to enjoy in this cursed world, and most of all on all the good that He has laid up for us in the world to come, which is preserved there for us (1 Peter 1:5). From all these benefits combined, we must try to make a lovely bouquet <note>original: "ruyckelken" - a small, fragrant bunch of flowers or a nosegay used for its scent</note> to smell and to taste how gracious the Lord is. This is so that we, through the bond of His manifold benefits—as if by a powerful love-potion <term>philtrum: historically, a potion or charm intended to excite the passion of love; here used metaphorically for God's overwhelming grace</term> or the compulsion of love—might be well-resolved to run constantly after the Lord like the Bride of Christ, drawn by the lovely fragrance of His name (Song of Solomon 1:3). We must cling to Him with all our strength and follow Him in all things, wherever He leads us, being drawn there by the bands and ropes of His love and kindness (Hosea 11:4).

And to that end we must (even when we think we have so much to do, and that today much work lies upon our hands) always consider this well: that the work of God <term>werck Gods: referring here to the inner spiritual duties of prayer and contemplation</term>, and the service of the Most High, is also a diligent work to which we must attend every day, and which we may never neglect. Therefore, we must always so prioritize our immediate business and work that might fall upon us now or then: that just as we see to it in such a circumstance—whatever work we postpone or set aside for that day—that we always see to practicing and completing the most necessary and useful task.

<column-break/>

We must also daily see to it that the Lord our God is never forgotten, and that His work (which is after all the most necessary) is never neglected or omitted. This is especially true because (when necessity requires it) this work can be done very quickly, simply through a strong resolution of our heart and the surrender of ourselves to God, and through faithful oversight, so that we then perform all our other affairs according to God's will and do not act perversely <note>original: "overdwerfen" — to act contrary or crosswise to a intended path</note> in them.

**Aquila.** I know by experience that a beautiful means to be strengthened against the world’s anxiety is that one frequently and earnestly considers that although toiling and laboring are reasonable means to provide for one's living (for we constantly see verified before our eyes what Solomon says, *a diligent hand makes rich*, **Proverbs 10:4**) it is nonetheless also the truth that even the best means cannot help in the least without the blessing of God: for *man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that God has spoken*. **Matthew 4:4**.

### Key of Devotion. 367, Book 4.

...it is also a work, that one provides for his household in time of need.

**Aquila.** How many excuses the flesh <note>In a theological sense, "the flesh" (original: *vleesch*) refers to human nature or worldly inclinations as opposed to the spirit.</note> can devise, so that it might be indulged in its desires! You ask whether one might say that, but you could see clearly enough (if only you would) that it does not fit the intention of Christ at all. For Christ is speaking there against those who, through anxiety <note>original: *sorchvuldicheyt*. This term implies both the practical "care" of management and the "worry" that distracts from God.</note> over arranging food and clothing for their household, neglected to seek the Kingdom of God and His righteousness. Thus, He makes a clear contrast between the care of providing for the necessities of one's household and the care of obtaining the Kingdom of God. And the care of a household's necessities shows itself in slaving and laboring (just as the Lord Christ also indicates through the parable of the **Lilies**, which do not labor), but the care of obtaining the Kingdom of God shows itself in the practice of **Spiritual exercises** <note>These "exercises" include prayer, scripture reading, and communal worship.</note>. Therefore, in this matter, properly speaking, he cannot be said 

<column-break/>

to seek the Kingdom of God who slaves and labors to provide for his household; for the Lord Christ sets these two in opposition to one another. And should anyone wish to say further that the Lord Christ speaks there only against an evil and excessive anxiety, that is precisely what we have now proven in this matter: namely, that it is an evil and excessive anxiety when we, for the sake of providing for our household, neglect to perform those **Holy exercises** through which the Kingdom of God is sought.

From this it then appears clearly enough that he who has the least opportunity is also to spend less time in spiritual exercises, such as those about whom you now ask. So, do not tell me much of godliness here and godliness there, but prove it to me with the facts; let it be shown in the faithful diligence of the work that God the Lord has laid upon each of us. For as it stands, I find that I am served just as well by a <term>slovenly woman</term><note>original: "ruyf-moesse." A term for a messy, unkempt, or careless person, particularly a servant.</note> who holds nothing at all of this 'devotion-bigotry'—or at least knows nothing of it—than by those who put on such a beautiful front and talk so much about how conscientiously they will do their work."

# Key of Devotion. Book 4

...indiscretion and a wrong misunderstanding, because they, hearing that one must seek the **Kingdom of God** above all else, and that the things of this world (which perish with use) are of no value, but that everything depends on the things of the world to come (which endure eternally), they judged that it mattered little whether they did their household work just as well, since it only concerned earthly, perishable things.

**Apollos.** Yes, I see well that even **Godly** hearts, if they do not watch carefully, can easily be ensnared and misled here by our **Spiritual** enemy. Therefore, I would also wish, **Theologian Aquila**, that you would briefly point out with one more word <unclear>how</unclear> one might lead the **Christian** person in this matter to balanced reflections.

**Aquila.** One must exhort such people that they should thoroughly consider that they are indeed bound by conscience to faithfully and diligently fulfill their daily housework (being the work of their <term>ordinary calling</term><note>In the 17th century, a "calling" or "vocation" referred to one's daily job or social role, which was believed to be assigned by God.</note>) before **God**; for the 

<column-break/>

**Lord** has also laid this upon the children of men for their humiliation, **Gen. 3. 19. Ecclef. 1. 13.** <note>Original: "Ecclef." refers to Ecclesiastes. Coll. 3. 22. 23. 1. Tim. 6. 1. 2.** Indeed, the **Lord** also counts the daily housework of the servants as His own work, and considers Himself served when they observe it conscientiously in obedience to His command, in such a manner as He has commanded. **Col. 3. 23. 24.**

So that the matters truly stand here in such a way that they cannot maintain a good conscience if they do not show good diligence and faithfulness in their daily housework: Yes, it is certain and sure that for those who now have the appearance of **Godliness**, the best and most evident proof that they also truly have the power of **Godliness** is this: That they are further found faithful and diligent in the work of their daily calling.

# Key of Devotion 581, Book 4.

# Ch. XXI. 584. Key of Devotion.

### Key of Devotion. 385. Book 4.

...also of private persons who are often also affected by it; namely, that the work inherent in that very calling is not better performed and fulfilled.

These people then (as anyone may see) do not clear their conscience well in this: nor do they do well by occupying that position so uselessly, and consequently keeping others out who might hold it and who ought to do better and fulfill it more than they do; which will be difficult for them to answer for on the last day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment.</note>.

And even if it were so that these people devoted themselves more abundantly to holy and religious exercises and contemplations, yet if that occurs with the neglect and omission of the work of their calling <note>original: *beroepinghe*</note> which they have accepted, they are not innocent in this regard: for as we have understood above in the general rules of discretion <note>The Dutch *bescheydentheydt* refers to the virtue of prudence, moderation, and knowing one's proper limits and duties.</note>, although the general divine services, exercises, and duties of godliness <note>original: *Godsalicheyt*</note> must be performed by everyone—of whatever calling he might be—with all faithfulness and diligence at their proper time: yet those particular...

<column-break/>

...and abundant contemplations of religious exercises stand open to a person only so far as he has completed all other particular and necessary work.

**Apollos.** So then you mean to say that one who accepts such a general calling in some way gives away his freedom, and having accepted it, is bound to make the best of it that he can for the greatest benefit of the common good <note>original: *ghemeyne beſten*</note>; and that he consequently must also reasonably occupy his mind with how he might conduct his calling most profitably.

**Aquila.** Yes, that is as it should be, and here one must pursue and keep in mind that which we have previously indicated regarding this in the discussion of the general rules of discretion.

**Apollos.** Since that is the case with public callings, I see well that it is no wisdom—when one can otherwise manage—to run so busily to pursue any office or public service.

### Chapter 21. Key of Devotion.

<margin>
Why it is also a great folly that people pursue public offices and positions with such burning ambition.
</margin>

**Aquila.** Yes, certainly; it is the greatest folly in the world to do such a thing if one only seeks oneself in it. For, whereas one who follows only a private calling (be it a shoemaker, or a tailor, or some such) may set the measure of his temporal business according to the sufficient provision of his household—of which we spoke before—he who accepts a public calling is, moreover, obliged to manage it so well that he produces as much convenience and benefit from it as is inherent in it for the **commonwealth**. And therefore, unless someone is assured on good grounds and with good judgment that he will be able to do more good in this or that public service—and also sincerely before God the Lord, who knows the hearts and reins <note>A biblical idiom referring to one's innermost thoughts and emotions; "reins" refers to the kidneys.</note>, intends to practice that very thing—than he can do in his private calling, it is not permitted for him to strive for any public service and thereby keep another out who might do better than he. For in public service, we may not take our private advantage or

<column-break/>

profit as the measure, but rather the common good and the public benefit; just as the nature of the matter undeniably demonstrates.

**Apollos.** How then do you hold it? Is a Christian person still free to strive for any higher state or position than he already possesses?

<margin>
This does not mean that a Christian should not act appropriately in their worldly and high office; on the contrary.
</margin>

**Aquila.** I believe that yes, the Christian person—without walking in things that are too great for him, as the Psalmist says in **Psalm 131:1** <note>original: "Heere! mijn herte is niet verheven... ick en wandele niet in dinghen die mij te groot zijn."</note>—can strive for it, provided he does so appropriately. For we read that it is permissible to desire the **office of a Bishop** <note>original: "Bisschops Ampt"</note>, **1 Timothy 3:1**, and consequently any other offices which, according to God's providence among the children of men, must be served by some for mutual convenience. And for these positions, none are now appointed through succession (as was the case with the priestly office among the children of Israel). For since these offices must be served by men, and no one in particular is appointed to them by birth, it stands open for everyone to prepare themselves for them and subsequently to test whether they might be promoted to this or 그 service.

<summary>Aquila explains that seeking public office out of personal ambition is foolish and morally risky, as public roles require prioritizing the commonwealth over private gain. However, he clarifies that Christians may still humbly aspire to higher positions if they are qualified and motivated by a desire to do good.</summary>

### Chapter XXI. The Key of Devotion.

...be advanced through good means. It is truly a matter that is much too high and too great for man if he attempts to force himself into a position through the dark, sinful way of flattery, of improper obligations, and of blinding gifts and presents. Is it not a dangerous thing to leave standing the path that God the Lord shows us, and instead to enter the path that Satan shows us? Is it not a matter too high and too great for us to want to climb into some higher state and service via the **black ladder** <note>A metaphor for achieving success through sinful or diabolical methods rather than divine favor.</note> that Satan himself throws up and holds? Let everyone take heed. Thus, this must also be firmly established among us—so that we do not make ourselves guilty of this reproach—that we do not walk in things that are too great and too high for us: that we in no way seek to force ourselves into any service through improper means, but only use good means to come to a good state.

**Apollos.** Dear friend, please tell us, what are the evil means that every Christian must guard against in this regard?

**Aquila.** The most prominent are

<column-break/>

these that now occur to us; though everyone who practices them knows best what goes on within.

1. That one seeks to advance oneself into the good graces of those whose vote we would like to win through all sorts of flattery, <term>sycophancy<note>original: "pluymstrijckinghe"; literally "feather-stroking," a Dutch idiom for bootlicking or excessive flattery.</note></term>, and fair-sounding speech to achieve our purpose. For that is to help oneself with the language of lies and with the harmful poison of the soul that can flow from the tongue of man.

2. That one seeks to win over, through material gifts and presents, those who might help us against others who perhaps have even better gifts than we do. That is an evil means. God the Lord condemns this in *Deuteronomy 16:19* <note>original: "Deut. 16. vers. 19"; this verse forbids taking bribes, as they blind the eyes of the wise.</note>. Paul did not wish to use such means to be released from prison, *Acts 24:26* <note>original: "Actor. 24. 26"; refers to the Roman governor Felix hoping for a bribe from the Apostle Paul, which Paul refused to give.</note>. And further, even granted that there are some cases where we may throw a morsel into the mouth of an unreasonable person—as if to a wild animal—to somewhat quiet their terrible raging, that nonetheless does not apply in this case where we speak of <term>promotion<note>original: "promotion"; advancement to a higher rank or office.</note></term> to higher positions. For in this case, it must always remain fixed for us: that we must not reach that goal except through a very straight path, if we intend...

Chapter 21. 592 Key of Devotion.

...to be promoted!
**Aquila.** These are principally the following:
1. Prayer to God. Before any work, commit your cause to God through prayer; indeed, labor toward this end, so that your cause might be granted to you in the Heavenly Court: and then hold this as certain, that it will then fall well here on earth, when a mandate or a prescription shall come from the High Court; then your affairs will stand well; otherwise, you must always assure yourself that, unless the Lord God finds it advisable to promote you to it Himself, it is neither useful nor <term>salutary<note>original: "salich"; meaning beneficial for one's soul or well-being.</note></term> for you to be promoted to it.
2. Then offer yourself to those who have the power from God to promote you: present your suitability for the service to them, and how you are fit for it: testify to them of your intention to desire to maintain a good conscience therein, and to uprightly seek the welfare of the <term>Commonwealth<note>original: "Republijcke"; referring to the state or body politic.</note></term> or Church, for your own part: do that as friendly and politely as you best can; and seek in every way to let them understand that they shall have in you a pious and faith-

<column-break/>

ful and diligent man in your <term>calling<note>original: "beroepinghe"; referring to one's professional vocation or station in life.</note></term>.
3. Having done that, wait upon the Lord for whatever outcome He wishes to give, and in the meantime neglect no occasions to stir up the favor of God and of the Lords toward you as much as you possibly can through the aforementioned two means.
See, this is how a Christian ought to conduct himself when there is an occasion to seek some advancement; if he does otherwise, he walks in things that are too high for him, he places himself in danger of a wretched fall, whereby he might grievously wound or entirely ruin his soul. See, this is how it ought to proceed.
**Priscilla.** It ought indeed to be so, but alas! we know well that it does not always go this way; indeed, that this is very distasteful to many, who believe that if all pious people wanted to follow this path, no pious man would ever be able to come into any office or station; that indeed, certainly the bold, the shameless, and the godless would run away with everything, and that all places, especially those of the Commonwealth, would be filled with unfit persons, to unspeakable damage.

## Chapter 24.

### General instructions regarding the discretion we must use in following religious contemplations, in view of the specific circumstances of our state of life.

**Aquila.** It is true; the aforementioned instruction can provide much light for that purpose, although we must otherwise acknowledge that it is nearly impossible to give a suitable literal instruction on this matter. The circumstances of people’s state of life, their needs, and the specific events of life are so manifold and so diverse; therefore, everyone especially needs, in those areas where they still feel somewhat doubtful, to bring a good and upright conscience to the matter, and then further to wait for and follow the special leading of the Spirit of God; which gladly leads all those who also possess an upright conscience in this regard. <note>See Romans 8:14 and John 16:13.</note>

**Apollos.** What do you call a "good conscience" here in this matter?

<column-break/>

hearts and kidneys <note>original: "herten ende nieren"; a biblical idiom for the innermost thoughts and emotions, often translated as "hearts and minds."</note>—to follow such a measure and rule in all these things as we are able to perceive, sustain, and feel, guided in our own conscience and mind, alongside God’s word and looking toward God’s word, as that which we are obligated to do.

### Apollos.

### Aquila.
I have also frequently experienced this in certain cases, and I know of no better advice for it than that we all keep ourselves suspicious of our own choices and hold the impulse of our own inclination as suspect. We must always see to it that we do not lean too heavily toward that side to which we feel ourselves strongly driven by our own inclination.

### Key of Devotion. 623. Book 4. ###

**Aquila.** Yes, that is what I mean to say; for example: if someone finds themselves consistently and particularly moved to be alone, and to that end to meditate on holy things, to study much, and so on; whereas another finds themselves particularly moved to be much among people, so that they might do good, admonishing the unruly, comforting the faint-hearted, and so on. In this case, both the one and the other must be cautious and well on their guard, and especially see to it that that humor <note>The "humors" were the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health and personality</note> (if I may call it that) which they find so strong within themselves, does not deceive them. And this must be considered all the more because the human mind <note>original: "gemoedt" – the seat of the soul's inclinations and emotions</note> functions just as the human body is found to function: in the body, one notices that the humor which is most abundant, and which begins to predominate <note>original: "predomineren"</note> there, vio-

<column-break/>

-lently exerts itself to turn all the sap and the vitality <note>original: "jeucht" – literally "youth," referring here to the body's vital nutrients or life-force</note> that is in the person toward its own humor and essence. Likewise, an excessive inclination and drive <note>original: "drift"</note> within a person’s soul toward this or that activity—even toward certain spiritual exercises more than others—is also always (though secretly) aiming to draw all of the person's powers more and more to itself. It seeks to bring it about that the person might apply all their senses, wit, understanding, and skill only to the carrying out of that one thing. Through this, it then happens that all other exercises are crippled and cut short. Thus, it begins to go with the soul of the person just as it goes with the body of those whose spleen <note>In early modern medicine, an enlarged spleen was thought to result from an excess of "black bile" (melancholy), which would eventually "consume" or waste away the rest of the body</note> grows and increases beyond measure, but at the cost of the oppression, wasting away, and sucking dry of all the other physical powers and members of the person. This is a very true test of the motive with which we go against or along with this or that person. For if we only stand for those who are of one <term>humor</term> with us, and otherwise clash <note>original: "dwers met de schoudere teghen"; literally "crosswise with the shoulders against," meaning to stubbornly oppose or obstruct someone.</note> with all those who are not exactly of our <term>humor</term>, even if they truly have something good...

<column-break/>

delight not in destroying human nature, nor in bringing it to nothing, but in sanctifying it and guiding it for the best. Consequently, the Holy Spirit gladly uses each person’s natural temperament, inclining and bringing the same to the best purpose. Thus, the Holy Spirit turns the <term>loftiness<note>original: "hovicheyt"; a natural sense of high-mindedness or pride.</note></term> that some people have by nature in earthly things into a holy boldness in heavenly things. Thus the Holy Spirit also teaches the <term>gentleness<note>original: "soetvoericheyt"; literally "sweet-conduct," an easy-going or mild disposition.</note></term> and the ease that many have regarding earthly things, turning it into a holy <term>tranquility<note>original: "vretredentheyt"; peacefulness or patient submission.</note></term>, endurance, and obedience to the hand of God in all spiritual things. Thus the Holy Spirit also guides the diligence and <unclear>fit</unclear>ness that some have by nature in not sparing their bodies in the pursuit of earthly things, turning it into a holy strictness of life in spiritual matters; so that they are much given to waking, fasting, and praying toward divine things. So it happens in this matter just as we see with water: it flows from one fountain, yet it greatly takes on the shape, color, and taste of the land or soil over which it flows, or of the channel in which it rests.

# INDEX,
## To the particular Books and Chapters of this Treatise.

### The First Book.
In which the foundation of Christian devotion is laid, in the true fellowship of our Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ.

**1. Chap.** Introduction to the following discourse: And that the Christian person ought also to conduct themselves in a Christian manner. **Page 1.**
**2. chap.** So that the Christian Person might conduct themselves in a Christian manner: Therefore they must consider that their principal work here on earth is: that they serve God the Lord according to His will, revealed in Holy Scripture. **page 4**
**3. chap.** In order that the person might be willing to set the course of their life according to God's will: They must often consider within themselves the things of the world to come, the state of Heaven and Hell. **page 9**
**4. chap.** That the person who is now willing to live Christianly must contemplate the fellowship of Christ, if they are to live a Christian life: And with what a great earnestness we are all equally bound to seek the fellowship of Christ, above all things in the world. **page 15.**
**5. chap.** Further explanation of what is necessary for us to live well and Christianly, according to our Christian profession: And namely of the Divine knowledge which we then need for that purpose. **page 27**
**6. chap.** Of humility <note>original: "ootmoedighedt"</note>, which is also necessary for us to lead a Christian life. **page 37**
**7. chap.** Of the faith that we have the highest need of in order to live Christianly. **page 44**
**8. chap.** Of the holy resolution to serve God the Lord in all things, which is also necessary for us to live well and Christianly. **page 53**

### The Second Book.
In which is shown the excellent state of our Lord Jesus Christ: and how wonderfully we are strengthened through the true knowledge of Christ, to deny ourselves: Together with how necessary, useful, and comforting the denial of self is: since we are thereby more and more advanced to the fellowship of Christ, and that the same is greatly advanced when we deny our flesh that which it most desires.

**1. chap.** How wretched the state of the natural man is, what a body of sin he carries about him, and how glorious and excellent the state of the Lord Christ is. **page 63**

<column-break/>

**2. chap.** How that by the vision and by the love of Christ, the body of sin is killed within us, and our hearts are drawn up from the earth toward Heaven. **page 68**
**3. chap.** How that by the vision and by the love of Christ, there are killed within us: pride, ambition, revengefulness, greed, sensuality, and other such cardinal sins <note>original: "hooft sonden"</note>. **page 73**
**4. chap.** How the sinful person, who has now received the vision of Christ's glory, dares to approach the Lord Christ, to be enlightened and strengthened through Him. **page 81**
**5. chap.** How the person must give themselves away and refrain from their evil desires, so that they might feel the good works of Christ. **page 82**
**6. chap.** How the Christian person must exercise themselves in denying certain particular cardinal desires of the flesh, which would otherwise hinder them in the race of Salvation. **page 86**
**7. chap.** How the Christian person must restrain and root out their outward and inward senses <note>Referring to the five physical senses and the internal faculties of the mind</note>, in order to deny themselves. **page 95**
**8. chap.** How necessary it is that the Christian person should deny themselves as discussed above, and that there are few who do so properly, even though it is very comforting. **page 98**
**9. chap.** That self-denial is at first wonderfully difficult to the flesh: and the reasons why: Together with how gladly the Lord Christ helps us therein: and how joyful it becomes thereafter, once we have broken through the hardest part. **page 101**

# Manuscript Binding

The front cover of this historical volume is bound in <term>vellum</term> <note>a durable material made from calfskin, common for important documents and books in previous centuries due to its longevity</note>. The material is heavily aged and mottled with brown and grey stains, showing minor scratches and surface wear consistent with its history.

On the right-hand edge, where the cover meets the spine, the horizontal binding cords and stitches remain visible, securing the pages within. There is vertical text handwritten in dark ink along this edge of the spine.
